terms.gloss: the unnamed provincial district town where the novel opens; 'uezd' is the pre-revolutionary county-level unit, still in use in 1927
terms.why_hard: the Gogolian 'town of N' convention must be kept as a letter, not expanded to a name; 'uezd' should read as a small county seat, not 'county' in the US sense

terms.gloss: protagonist, 52, former marshal of the nobility, now a registry-office clerk; the narrator almost always uses name+patronymic
terms.why_hard: transliteration and patronymic form must be fixed once (Matveyevich vs Matveevich); zh/ja need a stable multi-character transcription used identically hundreds of times

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビャーニノフ

terms.gloss: Klavdiya Ivanovna Petukhova, Vorobyaninov's mother-in-law, who sewed the jewels into the chair
terms.why_hard: she is referred to by name+patronymic only; translators must not add 'Mrs' or a surname the text withholds here

proposed.zh: 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜
proposed.ja: クラヴジヤ・イワノヴナ

terms.gloss: the town's coffin-maker, a recurring comic figure with a taxonomy of ways to die
terms.why_hard: surname appears in the chapter title; spelling must match across all chapters and the 'нимфы' rivals

terms.gloss: archaic trade title 'master of coffin affairs', i.e. undertaker/coffin-maker, styled like a pre-revolutionary shop sign
terms.why_hard: flattening to 'undertaker' loses the mock-solemn sign-board register that the narrator quotes

terms.gloss: the rival funeral parlour whose staff Bezenchuk calls 'the nymphs'; gives the chapter its title
terms.why_hard: the shop name must be kept as a proper name in quotes, and the plural 'нимфы' for its staff must be derivable from it in each language

terms.term: бюро похоронных процессий / похоронных депо / погребальная контора
terms.gloss: three pompous NEP-era euphemisms for a funeral business, varied deliberately for comic effect
terms.why_hard: a translator who normalises all to 'funeral home' kills the joke of bureaucratic over-naming; each variant needs its own stable rendering

proposed.en: funeral-procession bureau / funeral depots / burial office
proposed.zh: 殡葬仪式事务所 / 殡仪站 / 埋葬事务处
proposed.ja: 葬列取扱所 / 葬儀ステーション / 埋葬事務所

terms.gloss: name of a bankrupt funeral office; the phrase is a hospitable 'you are most welcome / do come in', grotesque on a coffin shop
terms.why_hard: must be translated as a phrase (the joke) not transliterated, and kept as a sign in capitals

terms.gloss: vegetal, a perfumed barber's hair lotion of the period
terms.why_hard: obscure even to modern Russians; should be rendered as a recognisable barbershop lotion, not a literal 'vegetable'

terms.gloss: mestkom = local trade-union committee; of the municipal-services workers' union
terms.why_hard: the acronym must expand to something a non-Soviet reader parses at once, and 'communal' must not suggest communists

proposed.zh: 市政公用事业工会基层委员会
proposed.ja: 公共事業労働組合の地方委員会

terms.gloss: trade-union membership dues collected by the local committee secretary
terms.why_hard: must stay recognisably union dues, not club fees or taxes

terms.gloss: street 'named after Comrade Gubernsky', a joke: the surname is the adjective 'provincial/gubernia'
terms.why_hard: the pun on 'gubernia' cannot be transliterated silently; keep the Soviet 'named after Comrade X' formula and preserve the name so the joke can be noted once

proposed.ja: グベルンスキー同志通り

terms.gloss: barbershop sign using the archaic 'tsirulnik' (barber-surgeon) and a fake-French owner name
terms.why_hard: the pretension is in the archaic title and the French 'Pierre' beside a plain 'Konstantin'; a flat 'barber' loses it

proposed.zh: “皮埃尔与康斯坦丁理容大师”
proposed.ja: 「理髪師匠 ピエールとコンスタンチン」

terms.gloss: mangled provincial gallicisms on a shop sign: manicure and ondulation (hair waving) at home
terms.why_hard: the comedy is the garbled foreign words; render as slightly pretentious salon-speak, not as correct modern 'manicure'

proposed.en: nail-grooming and ondulation at your home
proposed.ja: 爪のお手入れ、ご自宅で電髪

terms.gloss: to drink hard, be on a drinking bout (literally 'drink the bitter one', i.e. vodka)
terms.why_hard: a literal 'drank bitter' is meaningless; needs an idiomatic equivalent for heavy habitual drinking

terms.gloss: the (state) pawnshop of the NEP era
terms.why_hard: ordinary 'pawnshop' is fine but must be consistent, as pawning recurs as a plot device

terms.gloss: ZAGS, the Soviet civil registry office for births, deaths and marriages, where Vorobyaninov works
terms.why_hard: an acronym the target reader does not know; expand it rather than transliterate, and keep one expansion book-wide

terms.gloss: the 'desk' (sub-department) for deaths and marriages inside the registry office; 'стол' also puns with his literal table
terms.why_hard: 'desk' must be usable both as a department and as the physical table the next paragraph describes as a tombstone

terms.gloss: pince-nez spectacles clipped to the nose, Vorobyaninov's signature prop throughout the book
terms.why_hard: must be kept distinct from 'очки' (spectacles), since the passage contrasts them

terms.gloss: Pavel Milyukov, liberal Kadet leader and 1917 foreign minister, famous for his rimless spectacles; the wife's comparison is a slur
terms.why_hard: unknown to the target reader; needs a brief in-text gloss or note on why looking like him is undesirable in 1927

proposed.zh: 米留科夫（流亡的自由派政客）
proposed.ja: ミリュコーフ（亡命した自由主義派の政治家）

terms.gloss: the building yard-keeper, a low-status figure who sweeps, guards and reports; recurs across the novel
terms.why_hard: 'janitor' or 'doorman' each miss part of the role; choose one rendering and keep it

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's mood barometer: French greeting when cheerful, German when his liver aches
terms.why_hard: must remain foreign words in Cyrillic-style rendering, not translated to 'Good morning', or the contrast disappears

proposed.zh: “邦茹尔”（法语早安）/ “古特摩根”（德语早安）
proposed.ja: 「ボンジュール」／「グーテン・モルゲン」

terms.gloss: his liver is 'playing up', a colloquial hypochondriac's complaint
terms.why_hard: keep the light colloquial tone rather than a medical statement

conventions: Russian dialogue dashes become English double quotation marks, Chinese “ ” and Japanese 「 」; the narrator's parenthetical asides stay in parentheses in all three languages.

Name + patronymic is kept in full where the Russian has it (Ippolit Matveyevich), transliterated by a single fixed table; zh uses · between name parts, ja uses ・ and no honorifics (no さん) since the narrator uses none.

Soviet acronyms (загс, местком) are expanded to a plain descriptive phrase on first and every occurrence rather than transliterated; a translator's note is used only for allusions to real people (Milyukov) that no rendering can carry.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: The protagonist, former marshal of the nobility, addressed by name and patronymic throughout the book
terms.why_hard: Transliteration drifts (Ippolit/Hippolyte, Matveevich/Matveyevich); the name-and-patronymic form must be kept as one fixed unit in all three languages

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich's surname; Bezenchuk calls him 'господин Воробьянинов'
terms.why_hard: Surname contains воробей (sparrow) but must not be translated; spelling must match the patronymic form everywhere

terms.gloss: The coffin-maker of Stargorod, a recurring comic character who reappears later in the book
terms.why_hard: Recurring name; his dialect speech (ежели, неужто, значит) must get a fixed low-colloquial register that later pages reuse

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich's mother-in-law, Madame Petukhova, whose death opens the plot
terms.why_hard: Referred to by name-patronymic, as 'мадам Петухова', as 'теща' and as 'старушка'; all four must map to one person consistently

proposed.zh: 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜
proposed.ja: クラヴジヤ・イワノヴナ

terms.gloss: Chapter-title form of the mother-in-law's name; 'мадам' is a pre-revolutionary bourgeois honorific used mock-solemnly
terms.why_hard: Rendering it as plain 'Mrs' loses the deliberate old-regime flavour the narrator is mocking

terms.gloss: Mock-formal trade title, 'master of coffin affairs', modelled on pre-revolutionary guild titles like 'часовых дел мастер'
terms.why_hard: Flattening to 'undertaker' kills the pompous guild-title joke that the whole death-vocabulary scene builds on

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk addresses the ex-noble with the pre-revolutionary 'gospodin', anachronistic and obsequious in 1927
terms.why_hard: Must be kept distinct from 'товарищ' and 'гражданин' so the reader senses the old-regime deference

proposed.ja: ヴォロビヤニノフの旦那

terms.gloss: Orthodox formula said on hearing of a death, 'may she inherit the Kingdom of Heaven'
terms.why_hard: Literal rendering sounds like theology; it is a reflexive pious interjection like 'God rest her'

proposed.ja: 天国に召されますように

terms.gloss: Church-Slavonic verb for dying, first rung of Bezenchuk's ladder: for small, plump old women
terms.why_hard: The whole passage is a graded taxonomy of death-verbs; each rung needs its own fixed phrase that recurs later when Bezenchuk reappears

terms.gloss: 'Gives up her soul to God', for larger, thinner old women in Bezenchuk's taxonomy
terms.why_hard: Must be visibly different from 'преставилась' yet equally churchy; do not merge the two rungs

proposed.en: gives up her soul to God

terms.gloss: 'Played into the box', the death-verb Bezenchuk assigns to tall, imposing men like Vorobyaninov
terms.why_hard: Careless choice of 'kicked the bucket' here collides with 'дуба дал' later; the rungs must stay distinct and ranked

terms.gloss: 'Ordered (the rest of us) to live long', a genteel euphemism reserved for former merchant-guild men
terms.why_hard: Literal rendering is opaque; the point is a polite, bourgeois-sounding euphemism, not an order

proposed.ja: 皆に長生きせよと言い残した

terms.gloss: 'Keeled over' or 'stretched out his legs', the coarse rungs for yardmen and peasants
terms.why_hard: Two phrases for the lowest social rank; both must sound rougher than the merchant's and gentleman's phrases

proposed.en: keeled over, or stretched out his legs
proposed.ja: ひっくり返った、または足を伸ばした

terms.gloss: 'Gave the oak', the top rung reserved for the mightiest: railway conductors and bosses; recurs in the book as a catchphrase
terms.why_hard: This one is quoted back later and became a proverb; needs a memorable fixed rendering, not a generic 'died'

proposed.ja: 樫の木をくれてやった

terms.gloss: Low, dismissive death-verb Bezenchuk assigns to himself, 'a small man'
terms.why_hard: Must be the shortest and most contemptuous rung, below even the peasant phrases

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary merchant guilds (first, second guild), abolished by 1917; 'бывший' marks the man as an ex-person
terms.why_hard: The reader needs to see it is an abolished imperial rank, hence the 'former'

terms.gloss: Yard-keeper/house porter, a low urban occupation that recurs throughout the novel (Tikhon later)
terms.why_hard: 'Janitor' or 'doorman' misplaces the social station; a fixed word is needed because dvorniks recur

terms.gloss: Glazet, a silver-or-gold-threaded brocade used to line and cover coffins; Bezenchuk's upsell
terms.why_hard: Obsolete trade word; needs a concrete fabric name the reader can picture, and it recurs in the closing line

terms.gloss: Tassels on a coffin's cover, the other item of Bezenchuk's upsell ('с кистями')
terms.why_hard: Ordinary word for brushes/tassels; here it is coffin decoration and pairs with глазет

terms.gloss: Joke Soviet street name: 'Comrade Gubernsky Street', gubernsky meaning 'provincial', mocking renamings after obscure functionaries
terms.why_hard: Translating 'Gubernsky' loses the name; transliterating alone loses the joke; a fixed rendering plus one note

proposed.ja: グベルンスキー同志通り

terms.gloss: Central square of Stargorod, a recurring fictional location
terms.why_hard: Recurs across chapters; transliterate consistently, do not translate the 'Old Polish' etymology

proposed.ja: スタロパンスカヤ広場

terms.gloss: Fire-brigade chief, a German loan-title from the imperial service still used in the 1920s
terms.why_hard: Needs a single rendering here and for the firemen's song and Kolka 'брандмейстеров сын'

terms.gloss: The fire chief's name in the drunken song, a pun on насос (pump)
terms.why_hard: Speaking name: transliterate, but the pump joke is lost without a brief note or a rendered nickname

terms.gloss: Horse-drawn fire-brigade train of wagons with a pump and crew, pre-motor era
terms.why_hard: 'Fire engine' is anachronistic; the thin horses and canvas-legged men need a period image

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's 'diamond dreams' of the jewels; a recurring narrator's epithet with the old spelling брильянт
terms.why_hard: Recurs as a leitmotif ('ослепительные мечты' too); keep one fixed phrase across chapters

terms.gloss: Long sheepskin coat worn fur-side in, marker of peasant or tradesman dress
terms.why_hard: Recurs as Bezenchuk's costume; needs one concrete garment word rather than generic 'coat'

terms.gloss: Exasperated concession, 'the devil take you, have it your way'
terms.why_hard: Literal 'devil with you' is meaningless; it must read as a grudging yes

proposed.en: Oh, the devil take you! Go ahead!
proposed.ja: ええい、勝手にしろ！やれ！

conventions: Bezenchuk's ladder of death-verbs is a ranked taxonomy: fix one distinct phrase per rung in each language (преставилась < богу душу отдала < в ящик сыграл < приказал долго жить < перекинулся/ноги протянул < дуба дал, with гигнулся lowest) and reuse the same phrases wherever they recur in the book.

Forms of address are load-bearing: render господин / товарищ / гражданин as three visibly different words in every language (en Mr / Comrade / Citizen; zh 老爷 / 同志 / 公民; ja 旦那 / 同志 / 市民) and keep name-plus-patronymic as one unit, never shortened to a first name.

Russian dialogue dashes become standard quotation marks in en, 「」 in ja and “” in zh; Bezenchuk's rustic particles (значит, ежели, неужто) get a fixed low-colloquial register, while the narrator stays dry and mock-solemn with no added exclamation.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: The young con man protagonist; Ostap Bender, 'the great schemer'
terms.why_hard: Name must be fixed once across all three scripts; ja/zh transliterations of Ostap vary (オスタップ vs オスタプ, 奥斯塔普 vs 奥斯塔卜)

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility, now registry-office clerk; the second treasure hunter
terms.why_hard: Narrator alternates 'Ипполит Матвеевич' (name+patronymic, mock-respectful) and 'Воробьянинов'; both forms must be kept distinct and consistent, patronymic not dropped

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: Bender's recurring epithet: master of 'combinations', i.e. schemes and swindles
terms.why_hard: Literal 'great combinator' is meaningless in English; 'grand strategist' loses the con-man shade; must be one fixed epithet book-wide

terms.gloss: Petty shopkeeper mentality, penny-pinching (from лавочник, small shopkeeper)
terms.why_hard: Bender uses a class insult of the 1920s; 'shopkeeping' in English is neutral, the sneer is lost

terms.gloss: 'Learn to live on a grand scale' — Bender's motto of largesse with other people's money
terms.why_hard: жить широко is a set phrase; a literal 'live widely' is nonsense, and the line recurs as a Bender catchphrase

proposed.zh: 学着大手大脚地过日子吧！
proposed.ja: もっと大きく生きることを学びたまえ！

terms.gloss: Personal ledger account in Soviet bookkeeping; here Bender parodies accounting jargon (дебет, кредит, сальдо)
terms.why_hard: The joke is Bender's fluent misuse of bookkeeping terms; render with the standard accounting vocabulary of each target language, not with paraphrase

proposed.zh: 个人账户（借方、贷方、余额）
proposed.ja: 個人勘定（借方・貸方・残高）

terms.gloss: т. = товарищ, 'Comrade', the standard Soviet written abbreviation in documents
terms.why_hard: The abbreviation itself is part of the comedy (a monarchist writing 'Comrade' in his notebook); keep an abbreviated form, don't expand silently

terms.gloss: Date in the Russian clerical style: 25 April 1927, month in Roman numerals
terms.why_hard: Fixes the internal chronology of the novel; keep the Roman-numeral month look as a typographic trace of the notebook entry

terms.gloss: A 150,000-ruble venture — the estimated value of the jewels in the chair
terms.why_hard: The figure recurs; Bender's numbers (150,000; 60,000; 59,992) must be kept exact, not rounded, because the arithmetic joke depends on them

proposed.ja: 十五万ルーブルの大仕事

terms.gloss: Knitted woollen wrist-warmers, old-fashioned gentleman's underwear accessory
terms.why_hard: Not sports wristbands; the item marks Vorobyaninov as a fussy pre-revolutionary elderly man

proposed.ja: 毛糸のリストウォーマー

terms.gloss: 'Baronial boots' — Vorobyaninov's boots, the narrator's mock-aristocratic epithet for his pre-revolutionary wardrobe
terms.why_hard: Not a brand or type of boot; keep the ironic adjective rather than normalizing to 'fine boots'

terms.gloss: Jaeger-brand woollen underwear (after Gustav Jäger), a fashionable pre-1917 import; here darned and old
terms.why_hard: Not 'hunter's underwear' (егерь = huntsman); the brand name marks faded gentility

proposed.zh: 打过补丁的耶格尔牌羊毛内衣
proposed.ja: 継ぎの当たったイェーガー製の毛織り下着

terms.gloss: Уголовный розыск, the Soviet criminal investigation department (CID)
terms.why_hard: A Soviet acronym; English readers need a functional equivalent, and the same rendering must serve wherever the police recur

terms.gloss: Velvet 'Tolstoy blouses' — loose belted shirts worn by 1920s Soviet officials and intellectuals
terms.why_hard: Modern Russian толстовка means 'hoodie/sweatshirt'; a careless rendering gives Vorobyaninov nightmares about velvet hoodies

proposed.ja: ビロードのトルストイ・シャツ

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk, the undertaker of Stargorod; 'гробовых дел мастер' is his recurring shop-sign title
terms.why_hard: The mock-official title ('master of coffin affairs') is a running joke and must be rendered the same way each time it recurs

proposed.en: Bezenchuk, master of the coffin trade
proposed.ja: 棺桶職人ベゼンチュク

terms.gloss: The Butter (Oils and Fats) Trust, a NEP-era state trust; one of many -трест acronyms in the book
terms.why_hard: Trust-name coinages recur throughout; adopt one pattern (e.g. 'X Trust') so Маслотрест, Днепрострой etc. look like a family

terms.gloss: Gogol's Cossack hero; in Bender's dream he sells postcards of the Dnieper dam
terms.why_hard: The joke pairs a literary Cossack with Soviet industrialization; the name must be recognizable, and ja/zh should use the established translations of Gogol's title

terms.gloss: The Dnieper hydroelectric dam construction project, begun 1927, flagship of Soviet industrialization
terms.why_hard: An acronym for a construction site; 'Dneprostroi' means nothing to the target reader without the gloss 'Dnieper dam'

proposed.ja: ドニエプル水力発電所建設現場

terms.gloss: The yardkeeper: a live-in caretaker who swept the yard and street and reported to the police, a fixture of Russian urban life
terms.why_hard: Not 'janitor' (indoor) or 'doorman'; his 'direct duties' with the broom are the point of the joke

terms.gloss: 'Horse apples', i.e. horse droppings on the street
terms.why_hard: A literal 'horse apples' reads as fruit in zh/ja; the mock-elevated euphemism should be kept if the language has one

terms.gloss: Old women living in the almshouse (богадельня) next door, the 2nd Social-Security Home of chapter VIII
terms.why_hard: The word links to the almshouse plot; render as almshouse inmates, not generic 'beggars' or 'old women'

terms.gloss: Chapter VI title: 'Diamond Smoke', the treasure-fever haze in which the heroes dream
terms.why_hard: Old spelling брильянтовый (not бриллиантовый) is period colour; the title must match wherever the chapter is cited

conventions: Bender addresses Vorobyaninov with вы and mock-formal names; keep this distance in ja with です/ます and 〜たまえ, and in en by never letting Bender use contractions-heavy slang toward him
Russian dialogue dashes (—) are kept as em-dashes in en; zh uses “” quotation marks and ja uses 「」, one convention for the whole book
Soviet acronyms (угрозыск, Маслотрест, Днепрострой) are rendered by a short functional English/zh/ja name rather than transliterated, with a footnote only on first occurrence

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, former marshal of the nobility, now a registry-office clerk; one of the two chair-hunters
terms.why_hard: Name-plus-patronymic is the narrator's mock-respectful fixed epithet; it must be rendered identically every time, never shortened to Ippolit or replaced with a surname

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the young con man, the 'great combinator'
terms.why_hard: Spelling must be fixed once (Ostap not Ostup/Astap) and match the form used in dialogue and in the epithet 'великий комбинатор' elsewhere

terms.gloss: Fictional provincial capital ('Old Town'), Vorobyaninov's home town, setting of chapters 5-15
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed transliteration; do not translate as 'Old Town' or vary between Stargorod/Staryi Gorod; also stem of many acronyms (Старсобес, Старгико)

terms.gloss: The Second Home of the Stargorod Social Welfare Department: an old women's almshouse run by the local собес (отдел социального обеспечения)
terms.why_hard: Старсобес is a portmanteau acronym; a bare transliteration 'Starsobes' means nothing to the target reader, but a long official expansion kills the deadpan; needs a short fixed formula reused whenever the almshouse recurs

proposed.en: the Stargorod Social Welfare Home No. 2
proposed.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德社会保障局第二养老院
proposed.ja: スタルゴロド社会保障局第二養老院

terms.gloss: The yard-keeper's (дворник's) lodge in the courtyard of a town house; here Tikhon's basement room where Vorobyaninov lodges
terms.why_hard: Not a 'janitor's closet' or 'porter's lodge' in the Western sense; the дворник is a resident yard-keeper, and the word recurs as a location throughout the Stargorod chapters

terms.gloss: Bityug horses: a Russian breed of heavy draught horse used for carting
terms.why_hard: Translating as 'stallions' or 'steeds' loses the comic weight of huge cart-horses admiring their own hoofbeats; the image recurs on this page (золотые битюги, распустившиеся битюги)

terms.term: цифровая система (обучаю игре на гитаре по цифровой системе)
terms.gloss: Number-tablature method of teaching guitar to people who cannot read music, a stock small-ad of the period
terms.why_hard: Not a 'digital system'; the joke is a shabby correspondence-course advertisement

proposed.en: guitar lessons by the numbers method

terms.gloss: 'Social studies', the Soviet school and entrance-exam subject in Marxist civics that replaced history in the 1920s
terms.why_hard: Rendering it as 'sociology' misses that it is a Soviet-era exam subject; the joke is that it is required to enter a music school

proposed.ja: 社会科学（ソビエト式公民）

terms.gloss: People's Conservatory: 1920s open-admission music schools for workers
terms.why_hard: Reader should catch that this is a mass-education institution, not the Moscow Conservatory; keep 'People's' as the fixed marker for such 1920s bodies

terms.gloss: Red Army soldiers in budyonovka pointed cloth winter helmets
terms.why_hard: 'Winter helmets' suggests metal; the budyonovka is the iconic pointed felt cap and should get a fixed term (or a gloss) whenever Red Army uniform appears

proposed.en: Red Army men in pointed winter caps
proposed.zh: 戴尖顶冬帽的红军战士
proposed.ja: とんがり冬帽の赤軍兵

terms.gloss: Acronym for a Stargorod provincial communal/economic office whose shop fronts the puddle; one of the book's parodic Soviet abbreviations
terms.why_hard: Expansion is uncertain and the point is the sound of the acronym; needs one fixed policy for such made-up acronyms (transliterate and gloss lightly, or invent a matching English/Chinese/Japanese acronym)

terms.gloss: Provincial Planning Commission (губернская плановая комиссия), local arm of Gosplan
terms.why_hard: Must be consistently rendered with the same word for губерния used elsewhere in the book ('province'); plaster tigers and cobras on its pediment is the joke, so the name must stay short

terms.gloss: 'The district town of N.': the anonymous provincial town where the book opens, a Gogol/Chekhov literary convention
terms.why_hard: The letter N. is a classic Russian device; keep it as 'N.' rather than inventing a name, and keep 'district town' consistent with the opening chapters

terms.gloss: The White émigré who fled to Paris after the Revolution; Vorobyaninov later poses as exactly this
terms.why_hard: The target reader needs 'émigré' to carry the specific 1920s sense of anti-Soviet exile, not just a migrant; this seeds a running plot thread

proposed.en: an émigré just back from Paris
proposed.zh: 刚从巴黎回来的流亡分子
proposed.ja: パリから戻ったばかりの亡命者

terms.gloss: 'Lena Events Street', a street renamed after the 1912 Lena goldfields massacre of striking workers; a typical post-revolutionary renaming
terms.why_hard: 'Lena Events' is opaque without knowing it refers to a massacre; the joke is the bureaucratic euphemism, so the rendering should keep the euphemism and a short note may be needed

terms.gloss: Housing department of the local soviet, which allocated living space
terms.why_hard: Portmanteau (жилищный отдел); a fixed short form is needed since housing bureaucracy recurs across the Moscow chapters

terms.gloss: The fire watchtower whose lookout hung up black signal balls ('bombs') to show where a fire was burning
terms.why_hard: Literal 'bombs disappeared from the tower' reads as ordnance; the reader must see fire-signal balls, and the fire tower recurs later in the Stargorod fire-brigade scenes

proposed.en: the fire tower; its signal balls
proposed.zh: 消防瞭望塔；报警信号球
proposed.ja: 火の見櫓；火事の合図の信号球

terms.gloss: Great Pushkin Street, main street of Stargorod
terms.why_hard: Decide once whether street names are translated ('Great Pushkin Street') or transliterated ('Bolshaya Pushkinskaya'); Chinese and Japanese should follow the same policy

terms.gloss: The two planned tram lines, to the railway station and to the Privoz market (an Odessa name transplanted to Stargorod)
terms.why_hard: 'Privoz' is the famous Odessa market; a translator who renders it 'Delivery Line' loses the in-joke, while a raw transliteration needs the word 'market'

proposed.en: the Station line and the Market line

terms.gloss: Marx and Engels Street, another Soviet renaming of an old Stargorod street
terms.why_hard: Renamed streets are a running gag about the changed town; keep the deadpan and use the standard Marx/Engels forms in each language

proposed.ja: マルクス・エンゲルス通り

terms.gloss: Bohemian (window) glass, the standard high-quality pane glass carried by glaziers
terms.why_hard: Not decorative crystal; it is ordinary window glass in a glazier's box, so 'Bohemian crystal' would mislead

terms.gloss: Pupils of the 'first stage' (grades 1-4) of the Soviet Unified Labour School
terms.why_hard: 'First-step students' means nothing; needs 'primary-school' in target languages, consistently with any later school references

terms.gloss: 'Citizen', the neutral Soviet form of address/reference replacing 'gentleman'
terms.why_hard: Book-wide: гражданин/гражданка versus товарищ versus господин carry class and irony; each needs one fixed rendering in all three languages

terms.gloss: Idiom: 'every passer-by, all and sundry'
terms.why_hard: Literal 'oncoming and crosswise passers-by' is nonsense; use a target idiom of the same register

proposed.zh: 过往的形形色色的行人
proposed.ja: 行き交うありとあらゆる通行人

terms.gloss: A dandy, fop; here a provincial one in a suede cap with a yellow leather peak
terms.why_hard: Slightly dated, ironic word; the fixed rendering should be usable for the book's many NEP-era dressers

conventions: Personal names: transliterate (BGN-style) and keep name+patronymic wherever the narrator uses it; zh uses · between name parts, ja uses ・ in katakana; one spelling per character for the whole book

Soviet portmanteau acronyms (Старсобес, губплан, жилотдел, Старгико): render as a short descriptive phrase, never as a raw transliteration alone, except invented brand-like names (Старгико) which are transliterated; a note only on first occurrence

Street and institution names: transliterate proper-name streets (Bolshaya Pushkinskaya) but translate names that are jokes or slogans (Lena Events Street, Marx and Engels Street); zh and ja follow the same split

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: The young con man; co-protagonist, later styled 'the great schemer' (великий комбинатор).
terms.why_hard: Name spelling must be fixed once (Ostap not Ostap/Osip; Bender not Bendera); zh/ja transcriptions vary between published translations.

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility, now a provincial registry clerk; Tikhon's old master.
terms.why_hard: Narrator uses name+patronymic as a mock-formal marker; dropping the patronymic loses the tone, and zh/ja need one fixed long transcription.

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビャーニノフ

terms.gloss: The old yard-keeper of Vorobyaninov's former house, still loyal to his 'master'.
terms.why_hard: A peasant servant name; must not be confused with Patriarch Tikhon; ja should not add さん in narration.

terms.gloss: Chapter V title and Bender's book-long epithet: a master of shady 'combinations', schemes.
terms.why_hard: 'Combinator' is meaningless in English; 'smooth operator' is a common but idiomatic choice; must match every later use.

terms.gloss: Yard-keeper/porter of a townhouse, a pre-revolutionary post with quasi-police duties, still existing in the 1920s.
terms.why_hard: 'Janitor' or 'doorman' misplaces the role; the man lives in a lodge and reports to the house owner or the housing committee.

terms.gloss: The yard-keeper's lodge, a basement or ground-floor room where Tikhon (and now Ostap) lives.
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered consistently with дворник; 'janitor's closet' is wrong in scale and dignity.

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary 'master', a gentleman landowner as addressed by his servants; Tikhon still calls Vorobyaninov this in 1927.
terms.why_hard: The anachronism is the joke: rendering as 'boss' or 'sir' loses the old-regime flavor; zh/ja need a term with feudal overtones.

terms.gloss: A medal for long service as a yard-keeper, which Tikhon's master tried to obtain for him in St Petersburg before the war.
terms.why_hard: Tikhon's obsession recurs in later chapters; the reader must understand it is a Tsarist civil decoration that no longer exists.

terms.gloss: Pre-1914 name of the capital; Tikhon uses it because his story is set before the war (later Petrograd, then Leningrad from 1924).
terms.why_hard: Translator must keep 'St Petersburg' here, not modernize to Leningrad, since the old name signals Tikhon's dated worldview.

proposed.ja: サンクトペテルブルク

terms.gloss: 'The gentlemen officials', the imperial bureaucrats who refused the medal.
terms.why_hard: Господа is a pre-revolutionary honorific replaced by 'товарищи'; rendering flatly as 'officials' loses Tikhon's old-regime speech.

terms.gloss: The Tsar (Nicholas II), said to be abroad so the medal could not be granted.
terms.why_hard: Use the standard 'Tsar' consistently throughout, not 'Czar' or 'Emperor'.

terms.gloss: Revolutionary-era slang: shot, executed summarily (of the Reds shooting a gentleman).
terms.why_hard: Ostap's casual 'did they bump off your master?' must be flippant, not clinical ('executed').

terms.gloss: Contemptuous collective for soldiers, i.e. the revolutionary garrison of 1917.
terms.why_hard: Pejorative suffix -ня carries the master's disdain; 'soldiers' is too neutral.

terms.gloss: Ostap's pun on the pre-revolutionary romance 'Белой акации гроздья душистые' (fragrant clusters of white acacia), turning it into 'flowers of emigration'.
terms.why_hard: Untranslatable rhyme on a song the target reader does not know; needs a rendering that reads as a mock-lyrical quip plus a short note.

terms.gloss: White émigré, a Russian who fled abroad after the revolution; a politically loaded label in 1927.
terms.why_hard: Tikhon's retort 'Сам ты эмигрант' treats it as an insult; 'emigrant' in English lacks the White-Russian sting, 'émigré' carries it.

terms.gloss: The master's house was requisitioned by the Soviet state for an old women's almshouse (the 2nd House of Social Security, a recurring setting).
terms.why_hard: Not 'taken away by old women'; the passive 'забрали' is the state, and the almshouse is a Soviet social-security institution.

proposed.en: they took the house for an old women's home
proposed.zh: 房子被收去做老太太养老院了
proposed.ja: 屋敷は老婆たちの養老院に取られた

terms.gloss: Colloquial name for a ten-kopeck coin; Tikhon means the old women never tip him even that.
terms.why_hard: Render as a small coin the reader can size, not a bare transliteration; must be consistent with other coin names (пятак, двугривенный) elsewhere in the book.

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's pince-nez and his 'pre-war' (pre-1914) glow: his dyed black hair and moustache make him look like his old self.
terms.why_hard: 'Pre-war' must be understood as pre-World War I, and pince-nez is a recurring attribute of the character.

terms.gloss: Folk hospitality formula, 'welcome to our humble hut', delivered by Ostap with mock ceremony.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'hut' is odd; the cliché quality and mock-solemnity are the point, and Ostap reuses such formulas often.

proposed.ja: むさくるしいところですが、どうぞお入りください

terms.gloss: Literally 'smelled something frying'; idiom for sensing that money or a profitable affair is in the air.
terms.why_hard: English 'smell a rat' means suspicion of danger; here the sense is opportunity, closer to 'smell money'.

proposed.zh: 嗅到了有利可图的气味
proposed.ja: うまい話の匂いを嗅ぎつけた

terms.gloss: Kologriv, a tiny backwoods town in Kostroma province; Ostap names it as an absurd opposite of Paris.
terms.why_hard: The joke needs the name kept plus a hint of provinciality; do not localize to a target-language town.

proposed.zh: 科洛格里夫（穷乡僻壤的小城）
proposed.ja: コログリフ（片田舎の町）

terms.gloss: Morshansk, a provincial town in Tambov province; another mock guess by Ostap.
terms.why_hard: Same as Kologriv: keep the transliterated name consistent wherever it recurs.

terms.gloss: State Political Directorate (OGPU), the Soviet secret police in 1927; Ostap threatens Vorobyaninov with it.
terms.why_hard: Never expand into a neutral 'police'; the reader must feel the menace, so fix one abbreviation and explain it at first occurrence.

proposed.ja: ゲーペーウー（国家政治保安部）

terms.gloss: A registered letter; Ostap's absurd detail about a silk kerchief sent by his 'cousin in Paris'.
terms.why_hard: Not 'ordered letter'; and the deadpan bureaucratic precision is part of the joke.

terms.gloss: Ostap's orange-colored laced boots, a recurring attribute of his dandyish poverty.
terms.why_hard: Штиблеты are laced ankle boots, not 'shoes'; and 'orange' must stay as a recurring color epithet across the book.

conventions: Dialogue: Russian em-dash speech is rendered as quotation marks in en (double), zh (“ ”) and ja (「 」); the narrator's mock-solemn asides stay in the sentence, never footnoted.

ты/вы: Ostap says вы to Vorobyaninov and ты to Tikhon; render the gap through register (en: 'sir' vs. bare name; zh: 您/你; ja: です・ます vs. plain form), keeping Tikhon's speech rustic and deferential (ご主人様, 老爷).

Names: keep full name+patronymic in all three languages where the narrator uses it (Ippolit Matveyevich / 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇 / イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ); ja uses katakana with long vowels marked, no honorifics added in narration.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: A chair by the Gambs firm, the fashionable Petersburg furniture makers of the 19th century; the book's central object, always described by this epithet
terms.why_hard: Readers must recognise the same chair every time; 'Gambs' must be fixed as a brand name, not translated as 'Hamburg' or dropped as an adjective

terms.term: ореховый стул с гнутыми ножками, обитый английским ситцем в цветочках
terms.gloss: The recurring formula identifying the twelve chairs: walnut, bent (cabriole) legs, flowered English chintz upholstery
terms.why_hard: This formula is repeated near-verbatim throughout the book; it must be rendered identically each time so the reader can spot the chairs

proposed.en: a walnut chair with curved legs, upholstered in flowered English chintz
proposed.zh: 包着英国印花布的弯腿胡桃木椅
proposed.ja: 花柄のイギリス更紗を張った、脚の曲がった胡桃材の椅子

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, the former marshal of the nobility; the narrator almost always calls him by name and patronymic
terms.why_hard: The formal name-and-patronymic is part of the mock-solemn tone; reducing it to 'Vorobyaninov' or 'Ippolit' loses the joke and breaks consistency

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Surname of Ippolit Matveyevich; used by the narrator when the tone turns to fight-reporting
terms.why_hard: One fixed transliteration in each language; zh must not vary between 沃罗比亚尼诺夫 and other phonetic spellings

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor Vostrikov, the parish priest of the church of Frol and Lavr in Stargorod, the rival treasure hunter
terms.why_hard: 'Отец' here is a clerical title; 'Father Fyodor' must stay fixed and never become 'Fyodor's father' or 'Fedor' in one place and 'Fyodor' in another

proposed.zh: 费奥多尔·沃斯特里科夫神父
proposed.ja: フョードル・ヴォストリコフ神父

terms.gloss: Affectionate-respectful address to an Orthodox priest ('little father'); Ippolit's exclamation of recognition
terms.why_hard: Батюшка also means 'my dear fellow' or 'father' generally; here it identifies the man as a priest, so the rendering must be the clerical address

terms.gloss: 'Holy father', a Catholic-flavoured, sarcastic address Ippolit uses toward Father Fyodor
terms.why_hard: Must sound pointedly ironic, not like a neutral synonym for 'Father'; distinguish from батюшка by a colder register

terms.gloss: 'The ecclesiastical personage': the narrator's mock-official periphrasis for Father Fyodor
terms.why_hard: The comedy is bureaucratic solemnity; a plain 'the priest' kills it, an archaic 'the divine' misleads

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor's parish church, dedicated to the martyr saints Florus and Laurus (patrons of horses), in the folk form 'Frol and Lavr'
terms.why_hard: The folk form Фрол (not Флор) is the point; translators may 'correct' it to Florus or render two saints as one name

proposed.en: the Church of St. Frol and St. Lavr

terms.gloss: The itinerant knife-grinder's street cry, a stock 1920s urban sound
terms.why_hard: Should read as a recognisable street vendor's chant, not a sentence; zh has a ready equivalent in the classic Beijing cry

proposed.en: Knives to grind, scissors, razors to hone!

terms.gloss: The tinker's cry ('solder, mend'); пачинять is the dialect spelling of починять, echoing thinly after the grinder's bass
terms.why_hard: The misspelling marks a country tradesman's accent; a flat 'repairs' loses the echo joke

proposed.en: Pots to solder, kettles to me-end!

terms.gloss: A newsboy's slurred cry for the Moscow paper Izvestiya (organ of the Soviet government), garbled as 'Zvestie'
terms.why_hard: Both гайзета and Звестие are deliberate mispronunciations; rendering as a clean 'Izvestia' erases the street-cry humour, but the paper must still be identifiable

proposed.ja: 「モスクワの新聞、ズヴェスチヤ！」

terms.gloss: Smekhach ('The Laugher'), a Leningrad-Moscow satirical weekly of 1924-1928 to which Ilf and Petrov contributed
terms.why_hard: Real periodical; needs one fixed title in each language and should not be confused with Krokodil

terms.gloss: Krasnaya Niva ('Red Cornfield'), an illustrated literary weekly supplement to Izvestiya, 1923-1931
terms.why_hard: Real periodical; translating the title literally each time invites variant renderings ('Red Field', 'Red Meadow')

terms.gloss: A truck of Melstroy, the Soviet state trust for mill construction; one of the book's many NEP-era acronym organisations
terms.why_hard: A bare 'Melstroy' means nothing to the target reader; an in-line gloss is needed, and the pattern should match other -строй/-трест names in the book

proposed.en: a truck of the Melstroy mill-building trust
proposed.zh: 磨坊建设托拉斯的卡车
proposed.ja: 製粉所建設トラスト「メリストロイ」のトラック

terms.gloss: A Soviet militiaman, i.e. an ordinary policeman of the workers' and peasants' militia
terms.why_hard: 'Militia' in English suggests a paramilitary; 'policeman' loses the Soviet colour; one choice must hold book-wide

terms.gloss: The krakowiak, a fast Polish folk dance with hopping side-steps; simile for Ippolit dodging kicks
terms.why_hard: Should be recognisable as a dance name, not a place; zh and ja need a fixed transliteration

terms.gloss: The traditional Russian cry for help ('Guard!'), here whispered almost inaudibly by Father Fyodor
terms.why_hard: Literal 'Guard!' is opaque; the rendering must be the target language's stock cry for help, with the syllable-stretching preserved

terms.gloss: 'They're robbing [me]!', the impersonal Russian cry of a robbery victim, whispered rather than shouted
terms.why_hard: The comic point is a shout delivered as a whisper; keep it a stock exclamation, not a narrative statement

terms.term: Где же ваши усы? / А ваши локоны где?
terms.gloss: Mutual taunts: Ippolit's moustache was ruined by the Titanic dye and shaved; Father Fyodor cut his priestly long hair to travel incognito; the chapter title is drawn from this
terms.why_hard: Локоны are a priest's long locks, not ladies' curls; the exchange must echo the chapter title 'Где ваши локоны?' word for word

proposed.en: And where is your moustache? / And where are your locks?
proposed.zh: 您的胡子呢？/ 那您的长发呢？
proposed.ja: あなたの口髭はどこへ？／あなたの巻き毛こそどこへ？

terms.gloss: 'With a leopard's bound': the narrator's animal similes for Ippolit's sudden bursts of action
terms.why_hard: The mock-heroic simile should stay vivid and slightly absurd, not be normalised to 'quickly'

proposed.ja: 豹のようにひと跳びで

terms.gloss: 'The first position was restored': fencing/ballet terminology applied to two men clutching a chair, in the narrator's deadpan sports-report style
terms.why_hard: Must keep the technical, referee-like flavour; a paraphrase like 'they were back where they started' loses the parody

proposed.ja: 第一ポジションが復元された。

terms.gloss: Ippolit's genteel pre-revolutionary protest ('allow me, allow me'), used while prying fingers off the chair
terms.why_hard: It is polite ceremonial speech in an absurd context; 'let go' or 'excuse me' flattens the old-regime manners that define him

conventions: Dialogue: keep the Russian em-dash lines; en uses double quotation marks, zh uses “ ”, ja uses 「 」; narrator's interior thoughts in «» become en single quotes, zh “ ”, ja 「 」 with a following と思った where needed.

Names: en transliteration with -y- for й/ь (Vorobyaninov, Fyodor, Matveyevich); zh uses one fixed 新华社-style transliteration per name; ja katakana with long-vowel marks; name-plus-patronymic is never shortened when the Russian uses it.

Soviet acronym organisations (Мельстрой, Старсобес etc.): transliterate the name and add a 2-4 word in-line gloss on first use in each chapter, never a footnote; Ippolit and Father Fyodor address each other with вы, so zh uses 您 and ja uses です/ます with 神父 as the title, without stacking さん on it.

terms.gloss: The former marshal of the nobility, now a registry clerk; the narrator uses name + patronymic throughout, Bender uses surname or nicknames
terms.why_hard: Transliteration must be fixed once (Matveyevich vs Matveevich) and the formal name+patronymic must not be shortened to a first name

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇（沃罗比亚尼诺夫）
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ（ヴォロビヤニノフ）

terms.gloss: The young con man, 'the great schemer'; the narrator calls him Ostap, Bender, or by his mock titles
terms.why_hard: Fix one spelling; keep the narrator's alternation Ostap / Bender rather than normalising to one

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: The old yard-keeper of Vorobyaninov's former house, now a hard-drinking Soviet dvornik who still calls him 'master'
terms.why_hard: Speaks in servile pre-revolutionary register (барин, дружок addressed back as ты); his lines need a different register from Bender's

terms.gloss: Yard-keeper/caretaker of a courtyard building, in old Russia also a semi-police informer; here Tikhon's job
terms.why_hard: 'Janitor' loses the courtyard/gatekeeper role and the fact that he knows everyone's business; must be the same word every time

terms.gloss: Bender's name for the disastrous contraband hair dye (and for the whole moustache catastrophe); gives the chapter its title 'Traces of the Titanic'
terms.why_hard: It is a nickname, not the ship; keep the quotation marks and the same word wherever the dye or its aftermath is referred to

terms.gloss: The label-speak promise of the dye ('radical black'), repeated as a refrain as the moustache turns green
terms.why_hard: The comedy is the pompous advertising adjective; it must be rendered identically each time it recurs, not paraphrased as 'jet black'

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's habitual German 'guten Morgen', spelled in Cyrillic as he mispronounces it; a mark of his pre-revolutionary gentility
terms.why_hard: Must stay German (not 'good morning') and slightly mangled; the same spelling wherever the habit recurs

terms.gloss: 'Closed his drowsy eyelids' using the archaic poetic word вежды; mock-solemn narration
terms.why_hard: A flat 'closed his eyes' kills the joke; the narrator's Church-Slavonic/poetic register needs an equivalently elevated word each time it appears

proposed.ja: 眠たげな瞼を閉ざした

terms.gloss: Narrator's epithet for Vorobyaninov after the dye disaster ('the Titanic's victim')
terms.why_hard: One of many rotating epithets the narrator uses instead of the name; the epithet system must be preserved, not replaced with 'he'

terms.gloss: Bender's running name for the treasure hunt as a NEP-era 'concession' (a licensed private/foreign enterprise) and for the pair as 'concessionaires'
terms.why_hard: The book-long gag depends on one fixed word; it must sound like a business licence, not a moral concession

proposed.zh: 特许公司 / 特许合伙人
proposed.ja: 利権事業 / 利権組合員

terms.term: директор-учредитель концессии; главный руководитель работ и технический директор
terms.gloss: Mock corporate titles Bender assigns: Vorobyaninov is founder-director, Bender chief of works and technical director
terms.why_hard: The titles recur as epithets in narration; they must be rendered as fixed, deliberately bureaucratic phrases

proposed.en: founder-director of the concession; chief of operations and technical director
proposed.zh: 特许公司创办董事；工程总指挥兼技术总监
proposed.ja: 利権事業の創立理事；作業総責任者兼技術部長

terms.gloss: 'Like a soldier looking at a louse' - with hatred; a soldiers' simile Bender uses
terms.why_hard: Replacing it with a target-language idiom loses the barracks flavour; keep the image literal

proposed.en: like a soldier at a louse
proposed.ja: 兵士がシラミを見るような目で

terms.gloss: Street in Odessa where, per Bender, 'all contraband is made' - i.e. counterfeit imported goods; the line became proverbial
terms.why_hard: Reader needs to grasp that 'contraband' here means locally made fakes; transliterate the street and let Bender's sentence carry the joke

proposed.ja: マーラヤ・アルナウツカヤ通り

terms.gloss: 'Contraband goods' - in 1920s usage a boast of foreign quality, here exposed as a fake
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered so the pharmacist's boast and Bender's Odessa retort use the same word

terms.gloss: Primus kerosene pressure stove, the universal cooking device of 1920s communal flats
terms.why_hard: Not a 'gas stove'; a fixed rendering is needed since it recurs across the book as a domestic emblem

terms.gloss: Thieves' slang for a fake or forgery; here punning on липа = lime tree, since the moustache is now green
terms.why_hard: The pun (fake / green foliage) cannot survive literally; choose one fixed slang word for 'fake' and let 'green' carry the colour

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary 'master/landowner'; Tikhon still thinks of Vorobyaninov this way in 1927
terms.why_hard: The anachronism is the point; 'sir' or 'gentleman' loses the serf-to-master relation

terms.gloss: Asked for money for a hair-of-the-dog drink to cure his hangover
terms.why_hard: One Russian verb; a clumsy expansion breaks the deadpan rhythm, but 'asked for a drink' loses the hangover

proposed.en: asked for the price of a hair of the dog
proposed.ja: 迎え酒の金をねだった

terms.gloss: 'Hero of Labour', a Soviet honorific title of the 1920s; Bender applies it mockingly to the drunken yard-keeper
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered as the official title (capitalised) so the sarcasm registers, not as 'hard worker'

terms.gloss: Bender's ironic 'former colleague' for the relation between the ex-marshal and his ex-servant
terms.why_hard: Irony rests on the flat office word; do not correct it to 'former servant'

terms.gloss: Abbreviation of жилищный отдел, the local Soviet housing department that requisitioned furniture and flats after 1917
terms.why_hard: Soviet acronyms should be expanded to a plain functional name, not transliterated; same rule for all -отдел bodies in the book

terms.gloss: The supply/housekeeping manager of the No. 2 Social Security Home (an old people's home run by social welfare), i.e. Alkhen, who appears next chapter
terms.why_hard: Two acronyms (завхоз, соцобес) must be unpacked into one readable title and kept stable across the Stargorod chapters

proposed.en: the supply manager of Social Welfare Home No. 2
proposed.zh: 第二社会保障院的总务主任
proposed.ja: 第二社会保障ホームの管理主任

terms.gloss: 'Citizen', the neutral Soviet form of address replacing господин; Tikhon uses it after being bribed, contrasting with барин
terms.why_hard: Must be distinguished consistently from товарищ ('comrade') and барин; all three occur in this scene

proposed.ja: ヴォロビヤニノフ市民

terms.gloss: 'Comrade Bender' - Vorobyaninov's stiff, over-correct Soviet address to his partner
terms.why_hard: Keep 'Comrade' every time; dropping it removes the comedy of the ex-nobleman trying to sound Soviet

terms.gloss: 'The ice has started moving' - Bender's signature catchphrase announcing that a scheme is under way; proverbial in Russian
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed sentence for the whole book, recognisable each time; not 'the ice is broken' in the sense of small talk

terms.gloss: One-word oath of secrecy, 'the grave' - i.e. silent as the grave
terms.why_hard: A literal 'Grave' is opaque; render as the fixed idiom of secrecy while keeping it to a few words

proposed.ja: 墓場まで持って行きます

conventions: Dialogue: replace Russian em-dash lines with English double quotes, Chinese “ ” and Japanese 「 」; keep the narrator's bracketed asides inside the same sentence rather than as footnotes
Forms of address: render товарищ as Comrade / 同志 / 同志, гражданин as Citizen / 公民 / 市民, барин as the master / 老爷 / 旦那様, and never add Japanese honorifics (さん, 氏) that the Russian lacks
Soviet acronyms (жилотдел, соцобес, завхоз, etc.) are expanded into a short plain functional name in all three languages, never transliterated, and each acronym is bound to one rendering book-wide

terms.gloss: Chapter title; the fake monarchist conspiracy Ostap founds, name parodying Isaiah's 'swords into ploughshares' (перековать мечи на орала)
terms.why_hard: орало is archaic 'plough', not 'to yell'; the biblical echo and the pompous pseudo-White-Guard ring must survive; must match the chapter heading everywhere

proposed.en: The Union of the Sword and the Ploughshare

terms.gloss: The narrator's standing epithet for Ostap Bender, the scheming con man
terms.why_hard: Not 'combinator' (a logic term); pick one English epithet and use it every time, it is the book's most famous tag

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the protagonist con man
terms.why_hard: Transliteration must be fixed once; ja needs a stable katakana form

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, ex-marshal of the nobility, Ostap's partner
terms.why_hard: Name plus patronymic is the narrator's fixed form; do not shorten to a surname or add ja honorifics

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: 'Gentlemen of the jury' — Ostap's recurring mock-courtroom address, evoking the abolished tsarist jury trial
terms.why_hard: A catchphrase repeated across the book; must be identical each time and keep the absurd solemnity of addressing conspirators as a jury

terms.gloss: The homeless street children (besprizorniki) of the 1920s, a mass social problem and stock object of official charity appeals
terms.why_hard: 'Neglected children' misses the specific 1920s phenomenon; the pun 'беспризорные ... без призора' needs a matching repetition

terms.gloss: Soviet-era cliché 'children are the flowers of life', which Ostap parodies
terms.why_hard: Must read as a recognizable slogan so his 'flowers of the street / on the asphalt' variations land as parody

proposed.en: children are the flowers of life

terms.gloss: Ostap's mock-poetic labels for street children, riffing on the slogan above
terms.why_hard: Keep the same 'flowers' word as the slogan so the joke chains

proposed.en: flowers of the street / flowers on the asphalt
proposed.zh: 街头的花朵／柏油路上的花朵
proposed.ja: 街の花／アスファルトの花

terms.gloss: NEP-era bureaucratic label for white-collar workers and intelligentsia, 'proletarians of mental labour'
terms.why_hard: Should sound like official jargon, not a paraphrase like 'intellectuals'

proposed.ja: 頭脳労働のプロレタリア

terms.gloss: Old term for seasonal work away from one's village; here ironic for private sideline trade under NEP
terms.why_hard: Literal 'latrine trade' is wrong; it contrasts state employees (bread and butter) with private earners (caviar)

terms.gloss: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, the meddlesome locksmith-'intellectual' of Stargorod
terms.why_hard: His epithets (хлопотливый слесарь, слесарь-интеллигент) recur and must be stable

terms.gloss: Narrator's epithet for Polesov, the bustling, useless mechanic
terms.why_hard: слесарь is a fitter/locksmith, not a plumber; keep one adjective throughout

terms.gloss: Polesov's private label for Ostap, whom he takes for a young Guards officer of the White underground
terms.why_hard: Not 'young guard' (a Komsomol connotation); the pre-revolutionary Guards regiment is meant

terms.gloss: Ostap's joke on Polesov: 'a lone hussar with a motor', twisting the NEP tax category кустарь-одиночка с мотором (self-employed artisan using a motor)
terms.why_hard: The pun on кустарь (artisan) vs гусар (hussar) is lost unless the fiscal term is kept recognizable; may need a brief note

proposed.en: a self-employed hussar with a motor
proposed.zh: 带发动机的单干骠骑兵
proposed.ja: モーター付き個人経営の軽騎兵

terms.gloss: 'Bravo, hussar!' — Ostap mock-saluting Polesov as a dashing cavalry officer
terms.why_hard: Hussar must be the same word as in the pun that follows

terms.gloss: 'The merchantry' — Ostap's pre-revolutionary estate word for the NEP traders Dyadyev and Kislyarsky
terms.why_hard: The archaic estate term is the joke; 'businessmen' flattens it

terms.gloss: The уравнительный сбор, an equalization tax levied on private traders under NEP
terms.why_hard: A truncated tax name in speech; must be rendered as a tax, not 'the equalizer'

terms.gloss: Dyadyev's private firm, a NEP-style compound name meaning 'Quick-Pack'
terms.why_hard: Telescoped Soviet-style firm name; decide once whether to transliterate, calque, or both

terms.gloss: Kislyarsky, timid bagel-artel chairman who keeps joining conspiracies out of fear
terms.why_hard: Stable transliteration; his refrain ('золотая голова') recurs

terms.gloss: Dyadyev, owner of Bystroupak, the wealthiest Stargorod trader
terms.why_hard: Stable transliteration

terms.gloss: Charushnikov, former town-duma member, conspiracy member
terms.why_hard: Stable transliteration

terms.gloss: Elena Stanislavovna Bour, fortune-teller, Vorobyaninov's old flame, hostess of the meeting
terms.why_hard: Name plus patronymic form fixed; ja katakana must be consistent

proposed.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃芙娜
proposed.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ

terms.gloss: Nikesha and Vladya, two dim-witted young men in the conspiracy
terms.why_hard: Diminutive first names only; keep the pair order and the childish ring

proposed.ja: ニケーシャとヴラージャ

terms.gloss: Colloquial 'it's no concern of mine / I'm just a bystander'
terms.why_hard: Literal 'my business is sixteenth' is meaningless; needs an equally offhand idiom

terms.gloss: Ostap's light-blue waistcoat, a recurring costume marker
terms.why_hard: голубой is light/sky blue, not dark blue; keep one colour word across the book

conventions: Ostap's forms of address (Граждане / Товарищи / господа / господа присяжные заседатели) are rendered literally and distinctly every time — Citizens / Comrades / gentlemen / gentlemen of the jury (公民们 / 同志们 / 先生们 / 陪审员先生们; 市民諸君 / 同志諸君 / 皆さん / 陪審員の皆さん) — because his sliding between Soviet and tsarist registers is the joke.
Dialogue dashes become English double quotation marks, Chinese “ ”, Japanese 「 」; the narrator's deadpan asides stay in the sentence, unmarked, never moved to notes.

Personal names: English by standard transliteration (Vorobyaninov, Kislyarsky), Chinese by Xinhua conventions, Japanese in katakana with a middle dot between name and patronymic and no honorific suffixes added; name-plus-patronymic is kept wherever the narrator uses it.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, the former marshal of the nobility, now registry clerk; the narrator almost always calls him by name and patronymic
terms.why_hard: Dropping the patronymic or varying its spelling (Matveevich/Matveyevich) loses the mock-respectful formality that is the joke of the whole book

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーヴィチ

terms.gloss: The town coffin-maker, a recurring comic figure who prowls the town asking whether anyone has died
terms.why_hard: Surname must be transliterated once and kept; zh/ja must not vary between phonetic variants across chapters

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk's mock-solemn trade title, 'master of coffin affairs', modelled on old guild signage
terms.why_hard: Flattening to 'undertaker' or 'coffin-maker' loses the pompous shop-sign register; the short form 'мастер' recurs as his epithet

proposed.ja: 棺桶職人の親方（略：親方）

terms.gloss: The rival funeral parlour, run by three owners, with a pretentious classical name
terms.why_hard: Shop names in «» are jokes and must be translated, not transliterated, and rendered identically every time; the title of chapter I depends on it

terms.gloss: A now-defunct funeral parlour Bezenchuk remembers, named with the hospitable formula 'welcome, do come in'
terms.why_hard: The joke is a welcoming greeting on an undertaker's sign; a literal 'We beg your mercy' misses it

terms.gloss: A consumers' cooperative shop in the town, named in Soviet emblem style; a cock crows in it at noon
terms.why_hard: Must sound like a stock Soviet emblem name, not a pub; 'cooperative' here means a state-sanctioned retail shop, not a housing co-op

terms.gloss: A street renamed after 'Comrade Gubernsky', a name that literally means 'provincial'; parody of the mania for renaming streets after officials
terms.why_hard: Transliterating alone hides the pun, translating alone ('Comrade Provincial Street') breaks the realism; needs one fixed compromise

proposed.ja: グベルンスキー同志通り

terms.gloss: Uyezd (district) executive committee, the local Soviet government; its one decrepit car is a town landmark
terms.why_hard: Acronym must be expanded so the reader understands it is the local government, but consistently: the book is full of -ком/-исполком bodies

proposed.ja: 郡執行委員会の自動車

terms.gloss: State registration number 1, the licence plate of the committee's car; the joke is that the town's only car is 'No. 1'
terms.why_hard: Should read like an official plate designation, kept short and identical each time it appears

terms.gloss: The main square of the town of N, in front of the registry office and the Nymph
terms.why_hard: Recurring place name; zh and ja transliterations must be fixed once (not partially translated as 'Old Pan Square')

proposed.ja: スタロパンスカヤ広場

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov's desk in the civil registry office (ZAGS), which records births, deaths and marriages
terms.why_hard: The comic deadpan pairing of deaths and marriages must be preserved in that order; do not modernise to 'registrar's office'

proposed.ja: 死亡・婚姻登録係の机

terms.gloss: The registry ledgers in which the day's births and marriages are 'written down'; repeated as a refrain in one paragraph
terms.why_hard: The repetition is the joke; the phrase must be word-for-word identical each time, not varied for elegance

terms.gloss: Staff reduction, the standing terror of every Soviet office worker in the 1920s, invoked at the sight of the official car
terms.why_hard: Needs the bureaucratic ring of a formal measure, not casual 'layoffs'; recurs in the office world of the book

terms.gloss: 'Citizens', the neutral Soviet designation for townspeople that replaced pre-revolutionary 'gentlemen'
terms.why_hard: Rendering as 'people' loses the period flavour the narrators lean on; must be kept as 'citizens' throughout

terms.gloss: The jackdaws 'held a meeting/rally' over the square, a Soviet political verb applied to birds
terms.why_hard: A neutral 'circled' kills the joke; the verb must carry the political-meeting sense

proposed.en: held a brief rally over the square
proposed.zh: 在广场上空开了个群众大会
proposed.ja: 広場の上で集会をひらき

terms.gloss: Mock-ceremonious greeting formula ('honour to our dear guest') that Vorobyaninov uses to the coffin-maker
terms.why_hard: The formal old-fashioned register is the humour; a flat 'Hello' loses it

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk's signature euphemistic oath, literally 'there with her, into the swing'; a nonsense curse he repeats every few sentences
terms.why_hard: A recurring catchphrase; must be one fixed, slightly absurd phrase, not a different swear each time and not an obscenity

proposed.ja: ぶらんこに揺られちまえ

terms.gloss: Glazet, a silver- or gold-threaded brocade used for lining and covering coffins in pre-revolutionary trade
terms.why_hard: An obscure trade fabric; needs a real textile word (brocade), not a transliteration or 'cloth'

terms.gloss: The tassel on a coffin's drapery is 'thin' (skimpy); part of Bezenchuk's trade critique
terms.why_hard: кисть also means 'brush' or 'hand'; here it is the ornamental tassel

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk praises his coffin in grocer's language: 'a little cucumber' (fresh, first-rate), 'choice', 'gourmet grade'
terms.why_hard: The comedy is market-stall produce vocabulary applied to coffins; a bland 'excellent coffin' loses it, and the phrase recurs in his sales talk

proposed.en: a coffin like a fresh gherkin: choice, gourmet grade
proposed.zh: 我的棺材——像根鲜黄瓜，精选货，行家级的
proposed.ja: うちの棺桶はキュウリみたいにぴちぴち、選りすぐりの上物

terms.term: фирма старая. Основан в тысяча девятьсот седьмом году
terms.gloss: Bezenchuk quotes his own pre-revolutionary shop sign ('old firm, established 1907'), speaking of himself in the masculine as 'founded'
terms.why_hard: Must read like signboard language and keep the grammatical oddity of a man saying 'I was founded in 1907'

proposed.zh: 老字号。创办于一九〇七年

terms.gloss: Tver, the provincial capital near the town of N; a benchmark of quality in Bezenchuk's world
terms.why_hard: Use the historical name Tver (not Kalinin) and a fixed transliteration

terms.gloss: 'You will go dotty among your coffins', 1920s colloquial обалдеть = to be stupefied, lose your wits
terms.why_hard: Vorobyaninov is speaking gently (кротко), so the slang must be mild and avuncular, not abusive

proposed.en: You'll go soft in the head among those coffins
proposed.zh: 你在棺材堆里要待傻了
proposed.ja: 棺桶に囲まれて頭がぼけちまうぞ

conventions: Personal names: transliterate once and keep the Russian name+patronymic form in all three languages (en Library-of-Congress-style without diacritics; zh standard Xinhua transliteration with · between name and patronymic; ja katakana with ・); never substitute a given name where the Russian uses name+patronymic.
Business, cooperative and institution names in «» are translated (they are jokes), then fixed book-wide; en in italics or Title Case without quotes, zh in “”, ja in 「」.

Dialogue: replace the Russian em-dash dialogue lines with the target convention (en double quotation marks, zh “”, ja 「」); ты/вы asymmetry (Vorobyaninov ты to Bezenchuk, Bezenchuk вы back) is rendered in ja by plain form vs polite/rustic speech, in zh by 你 vs 您, and in en by register only.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the young con man; the narrator calls him by first name throughout
terms.why_hard: Transliteration must be fixed once (Ostap, not Ostap/Ostapp); zh/ja need one stable form used in dialogue and narration alike

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, ex-marshal of the nobility, always named by name-and-patronymic in narration

proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

proposed.en: we can always rearrange his face later
proposed.zh: 揍他一顿的事随时都来得及
proposed.ja: 顔をぶん殴るのはいつでもできる

terms.gloss: 'the mysterious rival' — the unknown competitor for the chairs (Father Fyodor), a label that recurs
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered identically each time so the reader tracks the running gag of the unseen rival

terms.gloss: A beer hall named after Stenka Razin, the 17th-century Cossack rebel and folk-song hero
terms.why_hard: The comedy is a proletarian pub bearing a folk-hero name; keep the proper name, do not translate it into 'The Rebel'

proposed.ja: ビヤホール「スチェンカ・ラージン」

terms.gloss: Eating zakuski (snacks) with drink — the standard Russian pub/table ritual
terms.why_hard: 'Had a snack' loses that drink is implied; 'had a bite over their beer' carries it

proposed.en: had a bite over their beer
proposed.ja: ビールをつまみと共にやる

terms.gloss: Housing department (жилищный отдел) of the local soviet, which allocated rooms and requisitioned furniture after 1917
terms.why_hard: A 1920s acronym; must be expanded to a plain 'housing office/department' and kept the same across chapters, since the chair trail runs through it

terms.gloss: The heavy dray horses (bityugs) that the sunset had gilded earlier in the chapter, now brown again at dusk

terms.gloss: 'Citizens', the Soviet replacement for 'ladies and gentlemen', used by the narrator for the crowd

terms.gloss: Street in Stargorod leading to the chemist's

conventions: Russian dialogue dashes become standard quotation marks: en double quotes, zh “ ”, ja 「 」; the narrator's deadpan asides are kept literal and never expanded into explanation in-text

Personal names: full name+patronymic transliterated (en BGN-style, zh 新华社 standard, ja katakana with ・), never shortened or replaced by 'Mr.'; nicknames in Russian quotation marks keep quotation marks in all three languages

conventions: Dialogue: Russian em-dash speech becomes double quotation marks in English, “ ” in Chinese, 「 」 in Japanese; narrator's mock-solemn asides stay in the same register as the surrounding sentence, never softened or explained inline.

Names: keep name + patronymic where the Russian has it (Viktor Mikhailovich), surname alone where it has surname alone; zh transliterates the full form with 中点 (·), ja uses katakana with ・, and Latin-script brand names (Indian, Wanderer) stay in Latin script in all three languages.

Address: Polesov's contemptuous ты to the carter is rendered with bare imperatives and an insult in en, 你 in zh, and plain-form commands (命令形) without honorifics in ja; polite вы between adults gets です/ます in ja and 您 only where deference is meant.
