terms.gloss: Chapter XII title; Ostap's mock-gallant label for the widow Gritsatsueva, which became a Russian catchphrase
terms.why_hard: It is a deliberately florid cliché, not a compliment; a flat literal title loses the mock-poetic register that the chapter's plot (Ostap marrying her for a chair) undercuts

proposed.en: A Sultry Woman, a Poet's Dream
proposed.zh: 热情似火的女人——诗人的梦想

terms.gloss: The narrator's standing epithet for Ostap Bender: the great schemer/operator
terms.why_hard: Recurs hundreds of times and must be one fixed phrase; 'combinator' is meaningless in English, while 'smooth operator' (Richardson) is one existing convention among several

terms.gloss: Former marshal of the nobility, co-hunter of the chairs; referred to by name-and-patronymic, surname alone, or 'Kisa'
terms.why_hard: Three alternating forms must map to three fixed renderings; spelling of the surname and patronymic must be identical throughout in all three scripts

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor Vostrikov, the priest who is the rival treasure-hunter
terms.why_hard: Narrative name 'отец Федор' vs. address form 'батюшка' vs. Vorobyaninov's sneer 'святой отец' are three different tones on one man; each needs its own fixed rendering

terms.gloss: Familiar, respectful address to an Orthodox parish priest ('little father')
terms.why_hard: Here it is said with 'inexpressible sweetness' by an enemy; over-explaining it as 'little father' sounds folksy, while 'Reverend' is the wrong church

terms.gloss: 'Holy father', used sarcastically in Vorobyaninov's thoughts about Father Fyodor
terms.why_hard: Must read as a jeer, not as a Catholic title; keep distinct from the neutral 'Father Fyodor'

terms.gloss: Ostap's mock-commercial name for himself and Vorobyaninov as partners in the chair 'concession' (NEP-era foreign-concession jargon)
terms.why_hard: A recurring joke in the voice of NEP business jargon; rendering it as plain 'partners' kills the parody, but the word must stay readable to a non-specialist

terms.gloss: Business partner, a semi-foreign NEP word used for Vorobyaninov from Ostap's viewpoint
terms.why_hard: Belongs to the same mock-commercial register as 'концессионеры'; should be a business term, not 'companion'

terms.gloss: The shabby Stargorod hotel where both parties lodge, pompously named after the Paris university
terms.why_hard: The joke is the grand name on a provincial flophouse; it must be recognisable as 'Sorbonne' in every language and stay in quotation marks as a proper name

terms.gloss: Hotel floor attendant who ran errands and carried linen (here, Alexander)
terms.why_hard: Not a modern 'bellboy' or 'porter'; a pre-revolutionary hotel job title that survives into NEP, needs one fixed word

terms.gloss: Soviet-era abbreviation for Soviet office employees (советские работники/совслужащие)
terms.why_hard: One of the book's many telescoped acronyms; the reader must feel the bureaucratic compound, not just read 'clerks'

terms.gloss: Telescoped name of a state mill-construction trust ('Mel'stroy'), owner of the overloaded lorry
terms.why_hard: An acronym-name typical of the 1920s; bare transliteration is opaque, full expansion is clumsy; decide one format for all such trusts in the book

proposed.zh: 磨坊建设托拉斯“梅尔斯特罗伊”
proposed.ja: 製粉所建設トラスト「メリストロイ」

terms.gloss: Stargorod's meddling 'intellectual locksmith', a recurring comic busybody who turns up wherever something breaks
terms.why_hard: Appears in many chapters, often just to 'give advice'; name must be spelled identically each time in all scripts

proposed.zh: 维克托·米哈伊洛维奇·波列索夫
proposed.ja: ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ・ポレソフ

terms.gloss: The ceremonial opening of the first Stargorod tram line, a running plot thread built by engineer Treukhov
terms.why_hard: It is a specific event in the novel, not generic transit news; render consistently with the earlier tram chapters (e.g. 'tram line', not 'streetcar' in one place and 'tram' elsewhere)

proposed.en: the opening of the tram line

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary and early-Soviet administrative district below the province (delegates 'from the uyezds')
terms.why_hard: Soon replaced by 'район'; the book uses both; pick one English word ('district') and do not confuse with 'county' connotations

terms.gloss: A long horse-drawn bench carriage used as a hotel shuttle
terms.why_hard: Not a 'line' or a 'ruler'; the 1920s provincial hotel still runs a horse wagonette with the hotel's name painted on it

terms.gloss: The furniture-allocation warrants (from the archive) that record where the Vorobyaninov chairs were sent; the paper trail the whole hunt follows
terms.why_hard: Not 'orders' in the military or shopping sense; it is a bureaucratic distribution voucher and must keep one term through chapters 11 onward

terms.term: согласно ваших полномочий … К сему прилагаю расписку
terms.gloss: Ostap's parody of office-memo language (with the incorrect genitive 'согласно ваших' typical of clerks) while dunning his partner
terms.why_hard: The humour is in the stiff bureaucratese spoken in bed; translate into stock office-letter phrasing, not natural speech

proposed.en: in accordance with the authority you conferred … Receipt attached herewith
proposed.zh: 根据您授予的权限……兹附上收据一份
proposed.ja: 貴殿の委任に基づき……なお、領収書を添付いたします

terms.gloss: 'To look at someone as a soldier looks at a louse': with hostile, blank scrutiny
terms.why_hard: The image is vivid and unfamiliar; keep it literal rather than replacing with a target-language idiom, so it stays in Ostap's voice

proposed.en: looking at me like a soldier at a louse
proposed.zh: 像士兵盯着虱子似的看着我
proposed.ja: 兵隊がシラミを見るような目で見る

terms.term: Не видать ему стульев, как своей бороды
terms.gloss: Twist on 'не видать как своих ушей' (you'll never see it, as you never see your own ears), with 'beard' substituted to mock the priest
terms.why_hard: A literal 'ears' rendering loses the beard joke; the target text needs the same 'as [he'll never see] his own beard' structure

proposed.en: He'll see those chairs the day he sees his own beard
proposed.zh: 他休想见到椅子，就像休想看见自己的胡子
proposed.ja: 自分の顎髭を見られぬのと同じで、椅子など拝めやしない

terms.gloss: 'He's stayed the fool he was' — reduplicative intensifier
terms.why_hard: Reduplication ('a fool of a fool') should be echoed rhythmically, not flattened to 'he's still stupid'

proposed.en: A fool he was and a fool he stays

terms.gloss: Traditional Russian side-fastening shirt worn with a cord belt; here the priest's off-duty dress
terms.why_hard: No target-language equivalent; a one-word transliteration needs a brief in-line gloss the first time, then a fixed form

terms.gloss: Pince-nez, Vorobyaninov's constant attribute (the narrator notes when he is without it)
terms.why_hard: Must be one word throughout since his 'eyes without the pince-nez' is a recurring image; avoid 'glasses'

terms.gloss: Menu-French 'soupe paysanne' as russified on provincial restaurant cards; the smell rising from a rubbish bin
terms.why_hard: The joke is the pretentious French label on garbage; keep the French menu form rather than 'peasant soup'

terms.gloss: The Orthodox Divine Liturgy (the morning service a priest celebrates)
terms.why_hard: 'Mass' imports Catholic colour; Chinese/Japanese Orthodox terms exist and should be used consistently for all church vocabulary in the book

chapter_titles.45: Глава XII. Знойная женщина — мечта поэта

conventions: Dialogue: Russian em-dash lines become “…” quotation marks in English and Chinese and 「…」 in Japanese; narrator's mock-solemn asides stay in the same sentence without added parentheses.

Names: keep name-and-patronymic where the Russian has it (Ippolit Matveyevich / 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇 / イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ), surname alone where the Russian has it; Chinese uses 新华社-style transliteration with ·, Japanese uses katakana with long-vowel marks, and neither adds honorific suffixes (no さん) except where Russian has батюшка etc.

Ostap's officialese and 1920s acronym-names (совработники, Мельстрой, концессионеры) are rendered in stiff bureaucratic register with a one-time in-line gloss on first occurrence, never a footnote; Orthodox church terms use Orthodox (not Catholic) vocabulary in all three languages.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: The 'great schemer', the con man co-protagonist; narrator alternates Остап / Бендер / Остап Бендер
terms.why_hard: Name must be transliterated identically whichever of the three forms the narrator uses; do not 'translate' Бендер

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, ex-marshal of the nobility, the other treasure hunter; the narrator uses name+patronymic constantly
terms.why_hard: Patronymic must be kept and spelled one way; zh/ja readers need a fixed short form so the pair name+patronymic is recognizable every time

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Family name of Ippolit Matveyevich; also appears as adjective (воробьяниновский особняк)
terms.why_hard: Adjectival form 'воробьяниновский' must resolve to the same surname, not a new word

terms.gloss: Varfolomei Korobeinikov, the fastidious old archivist who holds the furniture distribution records
terms.why_hard: Always 'гражданин Коробейников' in Ostap's mouth: the address form must be preserved along with the name

terms.gloss: Elena Stanislavovna Bour, Vorobyaninov's old flame, now a fortune-teller in Stargorod
terms.why_hard: Ostap claims to be her son by Vorobyaninov; the reader must link this name to the fortune-teller of earlier chapters

proposed.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜
proposed.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ

terms.gloss: Fictional provincial town ('Old Town') where the chase begins
terms.why_hard: A speaking name; transliterate, do not translate as 'Old Town', and use the same form in compounds like Старкомхоз

terms.gloss: The cheap Stargorod hotel (named after the Paris university) where the partners lodge
terms.why_hard: The joke is a flophouse called the Sorbonne; keep the recognizable French name and mark it as a hotel, not the university

terms.gloss: Railway workers' district on the outskirts of Stargorod where Korobeinikov lives
terms.why_hard: Real-sounding suburb name derived from 'goose'; transliterate consistently, not 'Goose Place'

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary style job title for a records clerk / archivist; used as Korobeinikov's epithet
terms.why_hard: Old-fashioned word chosen for comic dustiness; a flat 'archive employee' loses that

terms.gloss: Official distribution warrants recording to whom confiscated furniture was allotted
terms.why_hard: Not 'orders' in the command sense; they are allocation vouchers, and the word recurs through the whole plot

terms.gloss: Stargorod Communal Economy Department (Старгородское коммунальное хозяйство), the municipal housing/utilities office
terms.why_hard: Soviet telescoped acronym; needs one expanded rendering the reader can parse, then a fixed short form

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德市公用事业局（斯塔尔科姆霍兹）
proposed.ja: スタルゴロド市公共事業局（スタルコムホーズ）

terms.gloss: Housing department (жилищный отдел) that redistributed confiscated houses and furniture after the Revolution
terms.why_hard: Another acronym; rendering must make clear it is the office that seized and reallocated property

terms.gloss: Chancellery of the tsarist city governor (градоначальник), i.e. pre-revolutionary service
terms.why_hard: The joke is that Korobeinikov served every regime; 'mayor's office' hides that this is the old regime

terms.gloss: Marshal of the nobility (предводитель дворянства), Vorobyaninov's elected pre-revolutionary post
terms.why_hard: Not 'leader'; a fixed standard rendering must be used everywhere Vorobyaninov's past is mentioned

terms.gloss: 'Citizen', the neutral Soviet form of address that replaced 'sir' and is not yet 'comrade'
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed word in each language; dropping it removes Ostap's mock-official tone

terms.gloss: Morganatic marriage (royalty marrying a commoner); Ostap misuses it as a grand word for an illegitimate liaison
terms.why_hard: Translating as 'illegitimate' kills the joke; keep the pompous learned term

terms.gloss: French 'maman' as used by the pre-revolutionary gentry; Ostap puts it on to sound well-born
terms.why_hard: A plain 'mother' loses the affected French; keep a loanword

terms.gloss: Bureaucratic 'representation expenses' (entertainment allowance) that Ostap demands from Vorobyaninov
terms.why_hard: Ostap parodies office jargon; render with the target language's stock expense-account term

terms.term: маслом каши не испортишь / каша заваривалась
terms.gloss: Proverb 'you can't spoil porridge with butter' chained into 'a big porridge was brewing' (= trouble was brewing)
terms.why_hard: The narrator's pun needs both halves rendered with the same porridge image, not two unrelated idioms

proposed.en: you can't spoil porridge with butter / a big porridge was brewing
proposed.zh: 黄油多了不坏粥 / 一大锅粥正在熬起来
proposed.ja: バターで粥は駄目にならない / 大きな粥が炊きあがりつつあった

terms.gloss: Church Slavonic 'has reposed', Ostap's mock-solemn euphemism for 'died'
terms.why_hard: Register marker; a plain 'dead' flattens it, use an elevated religious euphemism

proposed.en: He has gone to his rest.

terms.gloss: NEP-era housing-cooperative apartment blocks, brand new and still damp
terms.why_hard: Not 'cooperative shops'; these are co-op housing built by member contributions

proposed.ja: 住宅協同組合のアパート

terms.gloss: Waistcoat of worsted (гарус) wool, Ostap's one item of finery
terms.why_hard: Obscure fabric word; pick one plausible cloth and keep it whenever the waistcoat reappears

terms.gloss: Embossed inscription on an old mechanical twist doorbell
terms.why_hard: Keep as an inscription in quotes, short and polite, so the period detail reads

conventions: Soviet telescoped acronyms (Старкомхоз, жилотдел): expanded descriptive rendering on first occurrence with the transliteration in parentheses, then the short form only.
Russian dialogue dashes become the target language's quotation marks (en "…", zh “…”, ja 「…」); narrator's asides stay in the sentence, no parentheses added.
Japanese: Ostap and officials speak in です/ます (mock politeness), the narrator in plain だ/である; no さん/氏 added to surnames, 'гражданин' is always 市民.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Fictional brilliant Petersburg hussar, count, later the monk Evpl; the 'hussar-monk' whose story Bender tells in ch. 12
terms.why_hard: The name recurs (Буланов / граф Алексей / граф-монах / гусар); one transliteration must be fixed and 'граф' rendered as a title, not dropped

proposed.zh: 阿列克谢·布拉诺夫伯爵
proposed.ja: アレクセイ・ブラーノフ伯爵

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the 'great schemer', protagonist of the novel
terms.why_hard: Bare surname here; must match the book-wide rendering of the protagonist's name

terms.gloss: Hussar, officer of the light-cavalry Guards regiments, byword for dashing dissipation in tsarist Russia
terms.why_hard: A generic 'cavalryman' loses the connotation of swagger and carousing the whole legend rests on

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary St Petersburg high society (the city is still 'Петербург' in the story, though the narrating present is Soviet)
terms.why_hard: Must stay 'Petersburg', not Petrograd/Leningrad, since the tale is set before 1914; the recurring epithet 'герой аристократического Петербурга' should be rendered identically each time

proposed.ja: 貴族社会のペテルブルグ

terms.gloss: English Embankment, the Neva quay of the grandest private palaces in St Petersburg
terms.why_hard: A literal 'English Quay' without context loses that this means the very richest addresses; keep the established place name

terms.gloss: Millionnaya Street, the aristocratic street beside the Winter Palace
terms.why_hard: The name itself says 'millionaires' row'; a bare transliteration hides the joke, a paraphrase loses the real street

terms.gloss: Society column of pre-revolutionary newspapers
terms.why_hard: Not 'secular chronicle'; it is the gossip/society page that Ilf and Petrov parody throughout the passage

terms.gloss: Frogging: rows of braided loops across the chest of a hussar's dolman jacket
terms.why_hard: Not a place name; the word is French 'brandebourgs'; a plain 'braid' misses the hussar uniform image

proposed.ja: 飾り紐（ブランデンブルク）

terms.gloss: Karakul (astrakhan) lambskin with a tight curl, trimming the hussar jacket
terms.why_hard: 'Grainy' is literal; the fur term is 'astrakhan'/'karakul' and 'tight-curled' describes the pelt

proposed.ja: 細かく縮れたカラクル毛皮

terms.gloss: Contemptuous officer slang for a civilian ('civvy')
terms.why_hard: A careless rendering gives 'beating up civilians' in neutral register; the word carries the hussar's sneer and needs a colloquial equivalent

proposed.zh: 老百姓（军官口中的蔑称）
proposed.ja: 民間人ども（軍人の蔑称）

terms.gloss: Negus Menelik II, Emperor of Abyssinia (Ethiopia), who defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896; Russian volunteer officers really did serve with him
terms.why_hard: 'Negus' is the Ethiopian royal title, not a name; the Italo-Ethiopian war of 1895-96 must be recognisable, and the joke is that Bulanov single-handedly 'routs the Italian king's army'

proposed.zh: 阿比西尼亚国王（尼格斯）孟尼利克
proposed.ja: アビシニアの皇帝（ネグス）メネリク

terms.gloss: The Abyssinian boy the count brings back as a page; recurring figure in the tale
terms.why_hard: The comic point is the homely Russian diminutive Vaska given to an Ethiopian; transliterate and keep the diminutive, do not 'normalise' to Vasily

proposed.zh: 阿比西尼亚小伙子瓦西卡
proposed.ja: アビシニア人の少年ワーシカ

terms.gloss: Russian General Staff map at three versts to the inch (1:126,000), the standard military map
terms.why_hard: Needs the unit 'verst' kept and the scale sense conveyed; 'three-mile map' silently changes the unit

proposed.zh: 三俄里比例尺军用地图
proposed.ja: 三ヴェルスタ図（軍用地図）

terms.gloss: Burnous, a hooded North African cloak
terms.why_hard: Keep the loanword; it is part of the pulp-adventure colouring of the Abyssinian episode

proposed.ja: バーヌース（フード付きマント）

terms.gloss: The count's last mistress; the surname is a joke, taken from the Belorussian-Baltic Railway (a Soviet railway administration of the 1920s)
terms.why_hard: Reads as a preposterous princely name; transliterate consistently and give a one-line note on the railway joke, and note the narrator later shortens it to 'Балтийская'

proposed.zh: 别洛鲁斯科-巴尔季斯卡娅公爵夫人
proposed.ja: ベロルースコ＝バルチースカヤ公爵夫人

terms.gloss: Fictional monastery; 'пустынь' is a hermitage-monastery in a remote place
terms.why_hard: Not 'desert'; the word is a monastic term and the name should be one fixed form

proposed.ja: アヴェールキー修道院

terms.gloss: Belshazzar of the Book of Daniel, whose feast is a byword for luxury; 'a nineteenth-century Belshazzar'
terms.why_hard: The Russian form Валтасар must be matched to the biblical name in each target language, not transliterated

proposed.en: a Belshazzar of the nineteenth century
proposed.ja: 十九世紀のベルシャザル

terms.gloss: Took the schema, the strictest Orthodox monastic vows
terms.why_hard: 'Took the schema' means nothing to the target reader; render as taking the strictest monastic vows, ideally with the term kept once

proposed.en: took the strictest monastic vows (the schema)
proposed.zh: 受了最严格的修士大戒（斯希玛）
proposed.ja: 最も厳しい修道誓願（スヒマ）を立てた

terms.gloss: Iron chains worn on the body by Orthodox ascetics; a pood is 16.4 kg
terms.why_hard: 'Chains' alone reads as prison; make clear they are penitential chains, and convert or gloss the pood

proposed.en: penitential chains weighing several poods (a pood is 16 kg)
proposed.zh: 几普特重的苦修铁链（一普特约16公斤）
proposed.ja: 数プード（1プード約16キロ）の苦行の鎖

terms.gloss: Monastic name taken by Bulanov, after St Euplus the deacon-martyr; chosen for its comic obscurity
terms.why_hard: Transliteration must be fixed once (the name recurs in the tale) and should look as odd in the target language as it does in Russian

terms.gloss: Klobuk, the tall cylindrical monastic hood with a veil; here fitted with a vertical peak covering the face
terms.why_hard: The joke is a monk inventing a uniform; the hood must be identifiably monastic and the modification identifiably absurd

proposed.en: a klobuk (monk's hood) with a sheer peak
proposed.zh: 带垂直面罩帽檐的修士高帽
proposed.ja: 顔を覆う垂直のひさし付き修道帽（クロブーク）

terms.gloss: Hegumen, abbot of an Orthodox monastery
terms.why_hard: 'Abbot' is clear; the Orthodox term should be used only if it is glossed

terms.gloss: Church-Slavonic register: 'possessed by pride' (pride as a deadly sin)
terms.why_hard: The mock-hagiographic tone is the point; a modern 'in his arrogance' flattens it

proposed.en: possessed by the sin of pride
proposed.ja: 高慢の罪にとらわれて

terms.gloss: High-society novels; the narrator flags his own cliché ('as they say in high-society novels')
terms.why_hard: The aside is a recurring device: the narrators quote a genre's clichés and then name the genre; keep the wink, do not cut it

proposed.en: as they say in high-society novels
proposed.zh: 正如上流社会小说里所说的那样
proposed.ja: 社交界小説の言い回しを借りれば

conventions: Pre-revolutionary ranks and titles (граф, княгиня, гусар) are rendered with their standard aristocratic equivalents (Count/伯爵/伯爵, Princess/公爵夫人/公爵夫人) and never modernised or dropped; the city stays 'Petersburg' in the tale of the hussar-monk.

Orthodox church vocabulary (схима, вериги, клобук, пустынь, игумен) is rendered with the plain meaning in the sentence and the Russian term given once in parentheses at first occurrence; no footnotes for these.
Old Russian measures (пуд, верста) are kept as loanwords (pood/普特/プード, verst/俄里/ヴェルスタ) with a metric equivalent in parentheses at first occurrence on a page.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: The 'Muse of Distant Wanderings' — chapter title and recurring mock-lyrical personification of wanderlust, quoting Gumilyov's poem 'Отъезжающему' (1913)
terms.why_hard: It is a literary allusion used with deadpan solemnity; flattening it to 'wanderlust' kills the recurring joke and the chapter title must match every later mention

proposed.ja: 遠き旅の女神（ミューズ）

terms.gloss: Railway right-of-way — the strip of land legally reserved for the railway; here used as a mock-solemn synonym for 'the railways'
terms.why_hard: Literal 'zone of alienation' sounds like Chernobyl; the narrator uses a dry legal-bureaucratic term where a normal writer would say 'the railway'

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor Vostrikov, the parish priest who is the third, rival treasure-hunter
terms.why_hard: Name and clerical title must be consistent book-wide; ja/zh must keep the Orthodox-priest sense (not a Catholic 'Father'/神父 only) and transliteration must match later pages

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, the former marshal of the nobility, now a registry-office clerk; protagonist
terms.why_hard: Name-plus-patronymic is used throughout as the narrator's mock-respectful form; the zh/ja transliteration must be fixed once and used for hundreds of occurrences

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: Marshal of the nobility — elected head of a province's or district's gentry in pre-revolutionary Russia; Vorobyaninov's former post
terms.why_hard: Not a military 'marshal'; readers need the sense of a gentry elected dignitary, and the epithet recurs ironically all book long

proposed.zh: 贵族首领（沙俄时代的贵族选任代表）

terms.gloss: Clerk of the ZAGS, the Soviet civil registry office for births, marriages and deaths
terms.why_hard: ЗАГС is an acronym unknown to the target reader; rendering must convey a dull civil-registry desk job, the comic fall from marshal of the nobility

terms.gloss: The anonymous provincial 'district town of N' where the novel opens — a Gogolian convention
terms.why_hard: The letter N must stay a letter (not be expanded); уездный is a pre-1929 administrative unit (district), not 'county' in the English sense

terms.gloss: Guberniya — pre-revolutionary and early-Soviet province, subdivided into uyezds
terms.why_hard: Must be distinguished consistently from уезд; 'Stargorod guberniya' recurs and the same word is needed each time

terms.gloss: Stargorod, fictional 'Old Town' — provincial city where the Vorobyaninov mansion and the chairs were, and where Ostap appears
terms.why_hard: Invented place-name; one transliteration must be bound book-wide, and the 'old town' pun should not be translated literally

terms.gloss: Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova, Vorobyaninov's mother-in-law, who revealed the jewels on her deathbed
terms.why_hard: Her death and registration is a set piece; the name must match earlier chapters and the recurring word тёща ('mother-in-law') should have one rendering

proposed.zh: 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜·彼图霍娃
proposed.ja: クラヴジヤ・イワノヴナ・ペトゥホワ

terms.gloss: 'Non-Party' — the standard Soviet form-field entry for someone not a Communist Party member
terms.why_hard: Read as parody of a Soviet death-certificate; 'non-partisan' or 'independent' misses that it means not a member of THE Party

terms.gloss: 'Of the nobility' — the old estate (сословие) classification of birth, absurdly still on a 1927 Soviet form
terms.why_hard: The joke is the collision of tsarist estate-language with Soviet paperwork; must be rendered as a formal category, not 'from a noble family'

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk, the coffin-maker/undertaker of the town of N, a recurring comic figure
terms.why_hard: His trade epithet is attached to his name every time; choose one word (undertaker vs coffin-maker) and keep it

proposed.ja: 棺桶屋のベゼンチュク

terms.gloss: A post-and-telegraph office — the standard Soviet local post office of the 1920s
terms.why_hard: Translators drop 'telegraph', but the compound is the period term and should be uniform wherever the post office appears

terms.gloss: The Aldan region in Yakutia, site of the 1923-24 Soviet gold rush
terms.why_hard: Without a hint the reader misses that 'running off to Aldan' means running off to the gold fields; needs a gloss-in-text or short note

terms.gloss: Works of Count Salias (E. A. Salias de Tournemire, 1840-1908), a prolific writer of pre-revolutionary historical potboilers, remaindered after 1917
terms.why_hard: The joke is that his once-fashionable books now sell for five kopecks; reader needs to know he was a popular hack, so a two-word in-text hint is needed

proposed.en: the collected novels of Count Salias
proposed.zh: 萨利亚斯伯爵的小说集
proposed.ja: サリアス伯爵の小説全集

terms.term: Провизор Леопольд Григорьевич, которого домашние и друзья называли Липа
terms.gloss: The pharmacist Leopold Grigoryevich, nickname 'Lipa'; провизор is a licensed dispensing pharmacist
terms.why_hard: Nickname Lipa must be kept as a name (not translated as 'lime tree'); провизор is a professional title, not 'chemist's assistant'

proposed.en: the pharmacist Leopold Grigoryevich, known to family and friends as Lipa
proposed.zh: 药剂师列奥波德·格里戈里耶维奇，家人朋友叫他利帕
proposed.ja: 薬剤師レオポルド・グリゴリエヴィチ、家族や友人にはリーパと呼ばれていた

terms.gloss: Fire chief — German loanword title for the head of a town fire brigade, still in use in the 1920s
terms.why_hard: The pompous foreign title is part of the provincial-notable comedy; 'fireman' loses the rank

terms.gloss: Brand-style cosmetics ('Ango' cream against sunburn and freckles; golden 'Rachel' powder for an even tan) — parodies of NEP-era advertising copy
terms.why_hard: The quoted ad text must read as advertising jargon in all three languages; brand names should be transliterated, not translated

proposed.ja: アンゴ・クリーム／ラシェル・パウダー

terms.gloss: A 'bug-boiler' — a kettle-like device for killing bedbugs with steam, built like a samovar but shaped like a watering can
terms.why_hard: Invented-sounding compound word; a translation must be a comic coinage too, and consistent if it reappears

terms.gloss: 'Titanic', the contraband hair dye whose 'radical black' turns green — recurring plot device for Vorobyaninov's moustache
terms.why_hard: Brand name must be kept as Titanic (the joke of a sinking ship) and the phrase 'радикальный черный цвет' rendered identically each time it is echoed

terms.gloss: 'Radical black colour' — the pharmacist's sales-pitch phrase, later mocked when the dye turns green; a proverbial line from the book
terms.why_hard: The mock-political adjective 'radical' should be kept literally so its echo in later chapters lands

terms.gloss: The 'accelerated' (semi-fast) train No. 7 — a Soviet railway category between passenger and express
terms.why_hard: Not an 'express'; the pedantic category name is part of the narrator's railway-timetable voice

terms.gloss: Train 'No. 1-K', the Moscow (Kursk station)–Tiflis express, given in timetable shorthand
terms.why_hard: Should be kept as a timetable designation, not expanded or mistaken for a name

terms.gloss: Tiflis, the period name of Tbilisi, Georgia
terms.why_hard: Use the 1920s name for period flavour, consistently, with the modern name only in a note if ever needed

conventions: Keep Russian dialogue dashes as em-dash-opened lines in en; use 「」 in ja and “” in zh; never merge the narrator's one-line asides into dialogue paragraphs.

Transliterate personal names once book-wide (en: Library-of-Congress-lite without diacritics, e.g. Fyodor, Vorobyaninov; zh: standard 新华社 transliteration table; ja: katakana with long-vowel marks) and keep name + patronymic wherever the narrator uses it.

Pre-revolutionary and Soviet administrative terms (губерния, уезд, загс, предводитель дворянства) get one fixed rendering each with a one-line translator's note at first occurrence only, never a footnote thereafter.
