terms.gloss: Chairman of the Stargorod municipal services board (Старкомхоз), Treukhov's patron and friend, drives the tram project through
terms.why_hard: Recurring name; must match the transliteration used in chapter XIII's opening pages, and his blunt worker-official register must stay distinct from Treukhov's

terms.gloss: The engineer who designed and built the Stargorod tramway after years of obstruction
terms.why_hard: Recurring; his shyness (заалелся, застенчиво) and sudden drunken eloquence must read as one character across pages

terms.gloss: The 'great schemer', the young con man co-protagonist
terms.why_hard: Name spelling must be fixed book-wide; zh and ja have established renderings from prior translations that readers may know

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: The former marshal of the nobility; Polesov addresses him with the pre-revolutionary honorific 'господин' plus name-and-patronymic
terms.why_hard: 'Господин' in 1927 marks Polesov as a nostalgic monarchist and frightens Vorobyaninov; 'Mr.' loses the danger, so it needs a marked rendering ('Mister Ippolit Matveyevich' or 'gospodin') applied wherever the word recurs

proposed.zh: 沃罗比亚尼诺夫 / 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇先生（旧称，含贵族口吻）
proposed.ja: ヴォロビヤニノフ / イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ様

terms.gloss: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, the manic Stargorod mechanic-intellectual and monarchist conspirator
terms.why_hard: Recurring; the narrator's epithets for him elsewhere (слесарь-интеллигент) must be coordinated with this spelling

terms.gloss: The narrator's running epithet for Bender and Vorobyaninov, from their mock 'concession' to hunt the chairs
terms.why_hard: A NEP joke (foreign concessions were real 1920s policy); must be one fixed word book-wide, not paraphrased as 'the pair' or 'the partners'

proposed.ja: 利権屋たち（コンセッショネール）

terms.gloss: A Soviet newsreel crew (кинохроника = state newsreel filming)
terms.why_hard: 'Chroniclers' or 'film historians' is wrong; it is a newsreel unit, and the capitalised 'Кинохроника' as a collective noun should read as 'the newsreel crew'

proposed.ja: ニュース映画の撮影班

terms.gloss: 'Jupiters': studio arc floodlights of the era, here in colloquial plural юпитера
terms.why_hard: A careless translator renders the planet or a brand name; it is film-set lighting jargon and should be a lighting term the reader recognises

proposed.zh: 聚光灯（当时称“朱庇特灯”）
proposed.ja: 照明ライト（ユピテル灯）

terms.gloss: Армяк is a peasant's heavy wool coat; the director wears an 'elegant leather sleeveless армяк', and the narrator then calls him 'the armyak-owner'
terms.why_hard: The joke is a peasant garment made into avant-garde leather fashion; 'coat' loses it, and the mock-bureaucratic compound 'армяковладелец' must be kept as a comic epithet

proposed.en: peasant smock (of leather, sleeveless) / the smock-owner
proposed.zh: 农民长褂（皮制无袖）/ 长褂主人
proposed.ja: 百姓外套（革の袖なし）／外套の持ち主

terms.gloss: Bender's coined label for flashy pseudo-fashionable style ('chic-moderne')
terms.why_hard: It is Bender's private idiom and recurs; render once as a mock-French tag and keep the quotation marks

terms.gloss: The director's stock command to non-actors; the chapter title, and now a Russian proverb for manufactured emotion
terms.why_hard: Must be identical in the chapter heading and every repetition on the page (three variants: with colon, with full stop, truncated); a literal 'breathe deeply' is fine but the imperative-plus-diagnosis rhythm must be kept

proposed.ja: 深く息を吸って——あなたは感動している！

terms.gloss: Film jargon: location/exterior scenery worth shooting
terms.why_hard: 'Nature' or 'a good model' misreads it; the director means they were distracted by a picturesque exterior (the sunset)

proposed.ja: いいロケ現場に出くわした

terms.gloss: Casting jargon of 1920s Soviet cinema (Eisenstein's типаж): a non-actor chosen for looking the social type
terms.why_hard: 'Type' alone is flat; the joke is that the boss Gavrilin is cast as 'a worker, a tram passenger' by appearance

proposed.ja: 申し分のないタイプ（典型）

terms.term: Крупно! / В три четверти / Войдите в рамку / Начали / Стоп
terms.gloss: Set-direction commands: close-up, three-quarter angle, into frame, action, cut
terms.why_hard: Each must be the standard film-set command in the target language, and the same each time it recurs

proposed.en: Close-up! / Three-quarter angle / Step into frame / Action! / Cut!
proposed.zh: 特写！/ 四分之三侧面 / 进入画框 / 开拍！/ 停！
proposed.ja: アップで！／斜め四分の三／フレームに入って／スタート！／カット！

terms.gloss: Komsomol, the Communist Youth League; the director stages a 'greeting from the Komsomol' scene
terms.why_hard: Komsomol needs one fixed rendering book-wide; 'Young Communist League' vs 'Komsomol' must not alternate

proposed.ja: コムソモールからの挨拶！

terms.gloss: 'Kisses!' — theatrical, gushing farewell used by the film director
terms.why_hard: Literal 'I kiss' is odd; it marks the director's affected showbiz register and should sound like luvvie talk

terms.gloss: Diminutives: Kolya the cameraman, Lyuda the actress; Милочка is both a girl's name and 'darling'
terms.why_hard: Diminutives must not be expanded to Nikolai/Lyudmila; 'Милочка' as a proper name should be transliterated, not translated as 'sweetie', or the reader loses who is being addressed

proposed.zh: 科利亚 / 柳达 / 米洛奇卡
proposed.ja: コーリャ／リューダ／ミーロチカ

terms.term: акробаты фарса, гиены пера, виртуозы ротационных машин
terms.gloss: Treukhov's drunken 'philippic' against the bourgeois press, a parody of Soviet newspaper invective; 'гиены пера' became a proverbial phrase
terms.why_hard: Must sound like inflated agitprop rhetoric, not real indignation; 'hyenas of the pen' should be kept literal since the phrase is famous

proposed.en: These acrobats of farce, these hyenas of the pen! These virtuosos of the rotary press!
proposed.zh: 这些闹剧杂耍艺人，这些笔杆子的豺狗！这些轮转印刷机的大师！
proposed.ja: この茶番の軽業師ども、ペンのハイエナども！輪転機の名手ども！

terms.gloss: Stock Soviet phrase 'the bourgeois press' as the target of a 'philippic' (learned word for a denunciation)
terms.why_hard: The comedy is the narrator's mock-solemn learned word for a drunk man's outburst; keep 'philippic' rather than 'tirade'

proposed.en: a philippic against the bourgeois press
proposed.zh: 一篇痛斥资产阶级报刊的檄文
proposed.ja: ブルジョア新聞に対する弾劾演説

terms.gloss: A bridge over the Hudson River; Treukhov's drunken engineering dream, echoing his earlier fantasies of bridges
terms.why_hard: River name must be recognisable ('Hudson', not transliterated 'Gudzon'), and it echoes his earlier bridge-building ambitions in the chapter

terms.gloss: A hired horse-cab driver, still the ordinary taxi of 1927 provincial towns
terms.why_hard: 'Taxi' is anachronistic and kills the irony that the tram-builder is driven home by horse; 'cab' or 'cabman' must be fixed book-wide

terms.gloss: Gavrilin's little lilac Fiat and the crew's Ford light truck (pickup)
terms.why_hard: Brand names in Russian quotation marks; the diminutive 'лиловенький' is affectionate-mocking and should be kept, and Ford/Fiat should be spelled as brands, not transliterated

proposed.en: his little lilac Fiat / a Ford pickup truck
proposed.zh: 他那辆淡紫色的小菲亚特 / 一辆福特小卡车
proposed.ja: 薄紫色の小さなフィアット／フォードの小型トラック

terms.term: депо / клуб / семейный вечер / рюмка водки
terms.gloss: The tram depot; the workers' club where the banquet is held; a 'family evening' (a private party); a small vodka glass (a shot)
terms.why_hard: 'Club' must not read as nightclub; 'рюмка' is a shot glass, three of which on an empty stomach explains the drunkenness

proposed.en: the tram depot / the workers' club / a family party / a shot of vodka
proposed.zh: 电车车库 / 工人俱乐部 / 家庭晚会 / 一小杯伏特加
proposed.ja: 車庫／労働者クラブ／家族の集い／ウォッカを一杯

conventions: Dialogue: Russian em-dash lines become double quotation marks in en, “” in zh, 「」 in ja; the narrator's asides and mock-solemn epithets (армяковладелец, концессионеры, кожаный режиссер) are rendered literally, never smoothed into plain description.

Forms of address: 'товарищ' = comrade / 同志 / 同志 (ja: 同志 as a prefix, no -さん); the pre-revolutionary 'господин' + name-patronymic is rendered with a marked, slightly archaic honorific (en 'Mister X', zh X先生, ja X様) so its political charge in 1927 is felt.

Names: keep diminutives as diminutives (Kolya, Lyuda, Milochka), never expand to full forms; name-and-patronymic address (Ippolit Matveyevich) is kept in full in all three languages, with ja using ・ between name and patronymic.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: The protagonist, Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, a former marshal of the nobility now a provincial registry clerk; almost always named by first name + patronymic.
terms.why_hard: The full name-and-patronymic form is itself part of the mock-solemn tone; shortening to 'Ippolit' or 'Vorobyaninov' loses it, and the transliteration must be fixed once.

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich's mother-in-law (his late wife's mother), a loud, stingy, dream-plagued old woman.
terms.why_hard: Name transliteration must be consistent; kinship must be rendered as wife's mother (not husband's mother) in Chinese and Japanese.

proposed.zh: 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺芙娜
proposed.ja: クラヴジヤ・イワノヴナ

terms.gloss: The coffin-maker who runs a shabby funeral shop across from the 'Nymph' and reappears through the book.
terms.why_hard: A recurring name whose folksy speech register must be kept consistent everywhere he appears.

terms.gloss: The rival funeral bureau, run by three partners; the 'nymphs' of the chapter title are its owners.
terms.why_hard: It is a shop name and a joke at once (nymphs vs coffins); must be quoted as a name and rendered the same way as in the chapter title.

terms.gloss: Master coffin-maker; an archaic guild-style trade title applied to Bezenchuk with mock dignity.
terms.why_hard: Plain 'undertaker' flattens the grandiose archaic formula; the rendering should sound like an old craft title.

terms.gloss: A small private funeral parlour of the NEP era, when such businesses were briefly legal again.
terms.why_hard: Should not become a modern 'funeral home' with a chapel; it is a tiny private shop.

terms.gloss: Klavdia Ivanovna's affected French-style pronunciation of 'Ippolit', marking pre-revolutionary gentry pretension.
terms.why_hard: Rendering it as a plain name loses the joke; each language needs a spelling that reads as the same name said with a French drawl.

terms.term: Слово «сон» было произнесено с французским прононсом
terms.gloss: The narrator notes that she nasalised the word 'dream' à la française, a gentry affectation.
terms.why_hard: The joke depends on the reader knowing French nasal vowels; the target languages need a brief way to say 'pronounced in the French manner' without a footnote.

proposed.en: The word 'dream' was pronounced with a French accent.
proposed.zh: “梦”这个词是用法国腔说出来的。
proposed.ja: 「夢」という言葉はフランス風の発音で言われた。

terms.gloss: French 'maman' as used by the old nobility; Ippolit addresses his mother-in-law with it, formally and coolly.
terms.why_hard: Translating as 'Mum' makes it warm and childish; it must read as a stiff old-regime form of address.

terms.gloss: Marie, Ippolit Matveyevich's deceased wife, Klavdia Ivanovna's daughter; she appears in the dream with loose hair and a golden sash.
terms.why_hard: The French form 'Marie' (not 'Maria') is part of the gentry colouring and should be kept.

terms.gloss: Pre-war (pre-1914) tailor-made trousers, sold singly rather than as part of a suit; a relic of better times.
terms.why_hard: 'Pre-war' must be understood as before WWI, and 'штучные' is bespoke/sold-by-the-piece, not 'odd' or 'fancy'.

proposed.ja: 戦前の仕立ての単品ズボン

terms.term: лунный жилет, усыпанный мелкой серебряной звездой
terms.gloss: A pale grey waistcoat with a fine silver star pattern, described in mock-poetic celestial terms.
terms.why_hard: The narrator's ironic ornament should be kept; it is not literally moon-coloured fabric but a fashion description made grand.

proposed.en: a moon-coloured waistcoat strewn with tiny silver stars
proposed.zh: 缀满细小银星的月色坎肩
proposed.ja: 細かな銀の星を散らした月色のチョッキ

terms.gloss: A jacket of lustrine, a cheap glossy wool-cotton fabric typical of clerks; the diminutive is condescending.
terms.why_hard: Lustrine is obscure; the rendering must convey cheap shininess and the diminutive's mockery.

proposed.zh: 一件闪光的亮纱料小上衣
proposed.ja: 光沢のあるリュストリーヌ地の小さな上着

terms.gloss: A castor (beaver-felt) hat, a pre-revolutionary gentleman's hat, here stained.
terms.why_hard: 'Castor' will be misread as castor oil; 'beaver hat' or 'felt hat' is needed.

proposed.ja: ビーバーフェルトの帽子

terms.gloss: Wife's mother; the diminutive 'тещенька' is Bezenchuk's fawning form.
terms.why_hard: Chinese and Japanese distinguish wife's mother from husband's mother; the diminutive must be rendered as obsequious, not affectionate.

proposed.ja: 義理の母（岳母） / お義母さま

terms.gloss: Yardmen (house porters who swept courtyards and kept order), absurdly playing harps in her dreams.
terms.why_hard: 'Janitor' or 'street cleaner' loses the old-Russian courtyard-keeper role; the incongruity depends on their lowly status.

proposed.ja: ハープを奏でる庭番たち

terms.term: архангелы в сторожевых тулупах, прогуливающиеся по ночам с колотушками
terms.gloss: Archangels dressed as night watchmen in sheepskin coats carrying wooden rattles (колотушки) used to signal rounds.
terms.why_hard: The rattle is a specific watchman's tool, not a mallet or club; the sheepskin coat marks the watchman's uniform.

proposed.en: archangels in watchmen's sheepskin coats, strolling at night with rattles in their hands
proposed.zh: 身穿更夫皮袄、夜里拿着梆子巡走的天使长
proposed.ja: 夜警の羊皮外套を着て夜に拍子木を手に歩き回る大天使たち

terms.gloss: Yellow piping of the dragoon regiments' uniform, here trimming dream-horses.
terms.why_hard: Military piping/braid terminology should be consistent with later uniform references in the book.

proposed.ja: 竜騎兵の黄色い縁取り

terms.term: Ричард Львиное Сердце, от крика которого, как известно, приседали кони
terms.gloss: Richard the Lionheart; the mock-erudite 'as is well known' cites a legend that horses squatted at his shout.
terms.why_hard: The 'как известно' irony must be kept; the legend itself is not common knowledge and the source should be checked.

proposed.en: Richard the Lionheart, whose shout, as is well known, made horses squat
proposed.zh: 狮心王理查——众所周知，他一声吼叫，马都要跪下
proposed.ja: リチャード獅子心王——周知のとおり、その叫び声で馬がひざを折ったという

terms.gloss: Whether the household water charge has been paid to the building/commune, a mundane 1920s domestic duty.
terms.why_hard: Not a water bill from a utility company but a communal payment; the flatness of the question is the comic deflation after the dream.

proposed.en: Have you paid for the water yet?
proposed.ja: 水道代はもう納めましたか？

terms.gloss: Rubber galoshes worn over boots, a standard item of Russian street dress.
terms.why_hard: Should be 'galoshes', not 'rubber boots'; they recur as a period marker.

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk's recurring folksy oath, a euphemistic curse roughly 'devil take it'.
terms.why_hard: It is a signature catchphrase and must be rendered identically each time; it should sound rustic, not obscene.

terms.gloss: A shopkeeper's ingratiating greeting, 'honour to the dear guest', shouted in a patter.
terms.why_hard: Literal rendering sounds odd; it needs a set fawning-merchant greeting of the same register.

proposed.en: Our respects to the honoured guest!

terms.gloss: Southern/Odessa slang (Yiddish-tinged) for trinkets, baubles; here dusty glass pendants on the lamp.
terms.why_hard: A colloquial, slightly contemptuous word; a neutral 'ornaments' loses the tone.

proposed.ja: ガラスのがらくた飾り

terms.gloss: Bezenchuk's lament about business losses, tied to his hope that the old woman will die and bring him a commission.
terms.why_hard: The dark joke (he wants a funeral) must remain readable without spelling it out.

proposed.en: nothing but losses, that's all we get
proposed.ja: 損ばかりでどれだけ食らってることか

conventions: Names: transliterate Russian names in English by a simplified Library of Congress scheme without diacritics (Ippolit Matveyevich, Klavdia Ivanovna, Bezenchuk); in Chinese follow Xinhua standard transliteration with the · separator; in Japanese use katakana with a ・ separator, and never add -san/-さん to names in narration.

Dialogue: replace Russian em-dash dialogue with English double quotation marks, Chinese full-width “ ” and Japanese 「 」; keep the narrator's asides (e.g. 'как известно', 'оказывается') as short deadpan parentheticals rather than smoothing them away.

Address: Ippolit Matveyevich and his mother-in-law use вы to each other; render as formal register (Japanese です/ます, Chinese 您), while Bezenchuk's folksy speech uses a consistently rustic, obsequious register in all three languages.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Engineer Treukhov, the chief engineer who builds the Stargorod tram line; earnest, competent, exasperated by the press
terms.why_hard: Transliteration must be fixed once (Treukhov, not Treuhov/Treykhov); he recurs across chapter XIII and later

terms.gloss: Pen name ('Flywheel') of the local journalist who writes bombastic industrial sketches about the tram construction
terms.why_hard: A speaking pseudonym: the mock-industrial name is the joke and pairs with Treukhov's rebuttal about 'transmission'; transliterating it alone kills it

terms.gloss: 'The Prince of Denmark' — the narrator's epithet for the same journalist, a Hamlet allusion set up earlier in the chapter
terms.why_hard: Must stay recognisable as Hamlet and be used identically each time it alternates with 'Makhovik'; readers must see both names denote one man

terms.gloss: Abbreviated 'Comrade' before a surname, standard in Soviet newspaper and official prose
terms.why_hard: Dropping it loses the newspaper register; abbreviating in English (Cde.) is opaque; Chinese and Japanese place 同志 after the name

terms.gloss: Chairman of the Stargorod communal services department, presides at the tram opening and comically gives himself the floor
terms.why_hard: Consistent transliteration across his several appearances in chapter XIII

terms.gloss: Soviet portmanteau for the Stargorod Communal Economy (municipal services) department
terms.why_hard: The acronym itself is part of the satire of Soviet officialese; needs one readable expansion plus one short form reused book-wide

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德市政局（斯塔尔市政局）
proposed.ja: スタルゴロド市営公共事業局（スタルコムホーズ）

terms.gloss: Provincial (guberniya) executive committee, the top local Soviet organ before regions replaced provinces
terms.why_hard: 'Provincial' vs 'regional' vs 'gubernia' must be settled once; the presidium of it sits on the rostrum here

terms.gloss: The fictional provincial town where the first half of the novel is set
terms.why_hard: Never translate as 'Old Town'; fix one transliteration and its adjective (Stargorod tram)

terms.gloss: Fictional outlying district of Stargorod where the tram depot is built
terms.why_hard: Odd Russian ending tempts inconsistent romanisation; fix once

terms.gloss: 'The concessionaires' — the narrator's recurring mock-business label for Bender and Vorobyaninov as partners in the treasure hunt
terms.why_hard: A book-wide running epithet playing on NEP-era foreign concessions; must not be flattened to 'the two friends' or varied

terms.gloss: Ninth anniversary of the October Revolution, 7 November 1926, a standard deadline for ceremonial openings
terms.why_hard: 'October' alone means nothing to the target reader; must expand to the Revolution and keep the date implicit

proposed.en: the ninth anniversary of the October Revolution
proposed.ja: 十月革命九周年記念日

terms.gloss: May Day, International Workers' Day, the other great Soviet ceremonial date
terms.why_hard: Keep its holiday sense, not a bare calendar date

terms.gloss: The Internationale, then the state anthem of the USSR, played three times by the brass band
terms.why_hard: Reader must know it is the anthem; keep the standard title in each language

terms.gloss: Raised reviewing stand/rostrum from which officials address a mass meeting
terms.why_hard: Not 'tribune' (a person) nor 'grandstand'; the same word recurs in every Soviet ceremony scene

terms.gloss: The presiding board of officials seated on the rostrum at a Soviet meeting
terms.why_hard: A Soviet ritual object more than a committee; keep one term across all meeting scenes

terms.gloss: 'Sketches of everyday life', a 1920s newspaper genre of feuilleton-style reportage
terms.why_hard: The genre label is what the narrator mocks; 'essays' or 'articles' loses that

terms.gloss: Page three of a Soviet newspaper, home of local and feature material
terms.why_hard: 'Column' or 'strip' is wrong; полоса means a page

terms.term: «15 000 рублей ржавеют», «Жилищные комочки», «Материал плачет», «Курьезы и слезы»
terms.gloss: Parodic newspaper headlines of the day ('15,000 Roubles Are Rusting', 'Housing Lumps', 'The Materials Weep', 'Curios and Tears')
terms.why_hard: Must sound like real earnest Soviet headlines, not jokes; keep the clumsy pathos, render each once and reuse if cited again

proposed.en: '15,000 Roubles Rusting', 'Housing Lumps', 'The Materials Weep', 'Curios and Tears'
proposed.zh: 《一万五千卢布在生锈》《住房的小疙瘩》《材料在哭泣》《奇闻与泪水》
proposed.ja: 「一万五千ルーブルが錆びている」「住宅の小さなしこり」「資材が泣いている」「珍事と涙」

terms.gloss: Truncated pre-revolutionary letter-closing formula ('Accept, etc.' — i.e. assurances of my respect)
terms.why_hard: Treukhov's curt use of an old-regime courtesy is the punchline; a modern 'Regards' or literal 'accept and so on' misses it

terms.gloss: 'The rafters hum' — Makhovik's bogus construction lyricism; стропила are roof rafters/trusses
terms.why_hard: Treukhov's rebuttal depends on the exact word; rafters must be rendered identically in article and rebuttal

terms.gloss: Journalist calls plain bolts 'transmission'; the engineer's rebuttal exposes the misuse
terms.why_hard: Keep both as recognisable engineering terms so the ignorance shows; do not smooth it

proposed.ja: トランスミッション / ボルト

terms.gloss: Thermite welding of rails, then modern technology, producing gapless track
terms.why_hard: Not 'termite'; the precise term signals the narrator's mock-technical exactness

proposed.ja: レールはテルミット溶接された

terms.gloss: 'Fittings/hardware' — the car works' quoted excuse for late delivery, in scare quotes
terms.why_hard: Not 'rebar' or 'armature'; the quotation marks signal a bureaucratic pretext and must stay

terms.gloss: 1920s colloquialism for a reflex camera hung on the chest
terms.why_hard: Anachronistic 'SLR' or literal 'little mirror' both wrong

terms.gloss: Newsreel cameramen from Moscow, whose arrival the provincial ceremony waits for
terms.why_hard: 'Chroniclers' misleads; it is newsreel film

proposed.zh: 莫斯科来的新闻纪录片摄影师
proposed.ja: モスクワのニュース映画班

terms.gloss: Cracking sunflower seeds, the emblematic idle pastime of a Russian crowd
terms.why_hard: Must specify sunflower seeds; 'seeds' alone puzzles the reader

proposed.ja: ヒマワリの種をかじった

terms.gloss: 'Brother of the pen', a fellow journalist
terms.why_hard: Keep the mock-elevated phrase rather than plain 'colleague'

terms.gloss: Journalistic cliché 'the crowd was all ears', written identically by two reporters
terms.why_hard: Must be a recognisable cliché in each target language so the identical-notebooks joke lands

proposed.ja: 群衆は耳をそばだてた。

terms.gloss: Sample of Makhovik's overwrought reportage rhythm, one-sentence paragraphs and present tense
terms.why_hard: Translator must keep the bad-prose register and paragraphing, not polish it

proposed.zh: 在我身后，屋架嗡嗡作响。
proposed.ja: 私の背後で小屋組がうなる。

conventions: Soviet acronyms (Старкомхоз, губисполком): on first appearance give a readable translated expansion with the transliterated acronym in parentheses, then reuse one short translated form; never leave a bare transliteration.

Quoted newspaper prose (Makhovik's articles, headlines, the reporters' notebook lines) is rendered in deliberately stilted officialese with its paragraphing kept; headlines use single quotes in en, 《》 in zh, 「」 in ja.
Abbreviated т. is always spelled out as Comrade in en and rendered as postposed 同志 in zh and ja; dialogue dashes become double quotes in en, “” in zh, 「」 in ja.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Treukhov, the engineer who designed and built the Stargorod tram and cannot make a speech
terms.why_hard: Spelling drift between transliteration schemes (Treukhov/Treuhov); he recurs across chapters 12-13 and must be one name

terms.gloss: Gavrilin, head of the Stargorod communal services department, Treukhov's boss and the tram line's political patron
terms.why_hard: Careless renderings lose the stress (Gavrílin) and vary the surname across pages

terms.gloss: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, the 'enthusiast-mechanic', a busybody locksmith who meddles in everything and finishes nothing
terms.why_hard: The narrator alternates 'Виктор Михайлович' and 'Полесов' in one paragraph; both forms must be recognisable as one man and the patronymic must not be dropped

proposed.zh: 维克多·米哈伊洛维奇·波列索夫
proposed.ja: ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ・ポレソフ

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, the former marshal of the nobility, one of the two chair-hunters
terms.why_hard: Long name with many possible transliterations; the book uses full name, first name + patronymic, and surname alone, all of which must map to one rendering

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比扬尼诺夫
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビヤニノフ

terms.gloss: 'former marshal' — short for предводитель дворянства, elected head of a district's nobility before 1917; the narrator's recurring epithet for Vorobyaninov
terms.why_hard: Literal 'leader' or 'chief' loses the pre-revolutionary rank; the ironic 'former' (бывший) is the whole point and must be kept every time

proposed.en: the former marshal of the nobility

terms.gloss: Comrade Mosin, a local official who gives the report at the club evening; 'т.' is the standard abbreviation of товарищ
terms.why_hard: The abbreviation is part of the parody of official print and should be rendered as an abbreviation or formula, not silently expanded to a first name

terms.gloss: Provincial Executive Committee (губернский исполнительный комитет), the top Soviet organ of a guberniya in the 1920s
terms.why_hard: Transliterating the acronym means nothing to the target reader; 'regional government' loses the Soviet flavour; the chairman must be an official, not a mayor

terms.gloss: The club and trade union of municipal (communal-services) workers — tram, water, housing staff — which hosts the celebration
terms.why_hard: 'Communal workers' suggests communes or communists; коммунальник means municipal-utilities employee

proposed.en: the Municipal Workers' Club / Municipal Workers' Union
proposed.zh: 市政工人俱乐部 / 市政工人工会
proposed.ja: 公共事業労働者クラブ／公共事業労働者組合

terms.gloss: Gusishche, a low-lying working-class quarter of Stargorod where the tram depot stands (recurs in chapters 12-13)
terms.why_hard: Fictional toponym; spelling must be fixed once and the '-ище' ending not turned into 'Gusishe' or 'Gusische'

terms.gloss: Bolshaya Pushkinskaya, the main street of Stargorod
terms.why_hard: Decide once whether street names are transliterated or translated ('Great Pushkin Street'); mixing both across the book is the common failure

proposed.ja: ボリシャヤ・プーシキンスカヤ通り

terms.gloss: 'Budyonny's March' (Pokrass brothers, 1920), the Red Cavalry anthem, the default festive brass-band piece of the 1920s
terms.why_hard: Reader must catch that it is a Civil War military song, hence comic when played out of tram windows; do not render as a generic 'march'

terms.gloss: 'The international situation of our state' — the stock opening of every Soviet public speech of the era, here delivered for the sixth time
terms.why_hard: Must sound like a worn formula in every language, and be rendered identically each time the book quotes a speech beginning this way

proposed.en: Comrades! The international situation of our state…
proposed.zh: 同志们！我们国家的国际形势……
proposed.ja: 同志諸君！　わが国の国際情勢は……

terms.term: акробаты пера, виртуозы фарса, шакалы ротационных машин
terms.gloss: The French communist's triple insult for the bourgeois press; became a Russian proverbial phrase for hack journalists
terms.why_hard: Ostap later quotes it; it must be kept as a memorable, quotable triad with the same wording wherever it recurs

proposed.en: these acrobats of the pen, these virtuosos of farce, these jackals of the rotary press
proposed.zh: 这些笔杆子杂技演员，这些闹剧名家，这些轮转印刷机的豺狼
proposed.ja: ペンの軽業師ども、笑劇の名手ども、輪転機のジャッカルども

terms.gloss: The Frenchman pitches parts of his speech on the notes A, C and E (solfège names)
terms.why_hard: Russian uses solfège; English readers know letter names, Chinese and Japanese readers know both — pick one system for the book and keep the orator joke

proposed.en: in A … in C … in E
proposed.ja: ラの音で……ドの音で……ミの音で

terms.gloss: To spout vague, muddy verbiage; Treukhov's verdict on Soviet oratory
terms.why_hard: Literal 'breed mud' is opaque; needs a colloquial verb for pointless waffle, and Treukhov's clipped inner voice must stay

proposed.ja: こっちはただ泥水をかき回すだけだ

terms.gloss: 'Copybook truths' — platitudes any schoolchild knows
terms.why_hard: The image is of handwriting-copybook maxims; a flat 'truisms' works but the book uses the phrase more than once, so fix it

terms.gloss: Tossing a hero repeatedly into the air by a crowd as a celebration; happens to Treukhov, Gavrilin, Mosin and twice to Polesov
terms.why_hard: 'Rocked' or 'swung' misreads it; English needs 'tossed in the air'; Japanese has an exact custom (胴上げ), Chinese needs a descriptive phrase

terms.gloss: About six poods: 1 pood = 16.38 kg, so Gavrilin weighs roughly 100 kg
terms.why_hard: Decide once whether old Russian units are kept (pood, verst, arshin) with a conversion or converted outright; technical readers will want the number

proposed.en: a good six poods (nearly a hundred kilos)
proposed.zh: 足有六普特（近一百公斤）

terms.gloss: Tram driver (period term, distinct from the conductor who sells tickets)
terms.why_hard: Must be kept distinct from кондуктор; 'motorman' is the period English term, 'driver' is acceptable if used consistently

terms.term: Воздушный тормоз … не всасывает / авось засосет
terms.gloss: Polesov's pseudo-expert complaint that the air brake 'isn't sucking', and the driver's fatalistic 'авось' (maybe, with luck) retort
terms.why_hard: The joke is that air brakes do not suck; the translation must let the nonsense stand and keep авось as a shrug, not a promise

proposed.en: "The air brake isn't up to much — it doesn't suck." / "Nobody asked you. Maybe it'll get sucking yet."
proposed.zh: “气闸不太灵——吸不上来。”／“没人问你，说不定过会儿就吸上了。”
proposed.ja: 「空気ブレーキの調子が悪いな、吸い込まん」／「誰も聞いとらんよ。まあ、そのうち吸うだろう」

terms.gloss: Stiff chancery participle 'which is to take place', typical of printed invitations and Soviet office prose
terms.why_hard: The invitation card is a parody of official typography; rendering it in plain speech kills the joke — use an equally stiff formula

terms.gloss: The 'unofficial part' of a Soviet public event: concert and supper after the reports and award ceremony
terms.why_hard: Standard programme heading of the era; should read as a heading, and the same rendering must be used whenever a programme is printed in the book

terms.gloss: Presentation of a грамота — a printed certificate of honour awarded by a union or institution
terms.why_hard: 'Diploma' or 'charter' mislead; it is an honorary certificate, a peculiarly Soviet ritual object

proposed.en: Presentation of a certificate of honour

terms.gloss: Polesov takes Ostap for an ex-(White) officer — one of the 'former people' of the 1920s; the phrase drives his conspiratorial plot
terms.why_hard: 'Former officer' must carry the whiff of the old regime; 'retired officer' or 'veteran' destroys the implication

terms.gloss: Chapter XIII title; a mock-medical exhortation that became proverbial in Russian
terms.why_hard: Must sound like a doctor's or official's soothing formula and remain quotable; keep the colon and exclamation

proposed.ja: 深呼吸を。あなたは興奮しています！

conventions: Soviet acronyms (губисполком, and later Старкомхоз etc.) are rendered as expanded plain institution names, never as transliterated acronyms; the Russian acronym may be shown once in a bracket at first occurrence only.

Dialogue dashes become en "…" quotation marks, zh “…” full-width quotes, ja 「…」; the narrator's italic-free inner speech in «» becomes en single quotes, zh “”, ja 「」, kept distinct from spoken lines only by the reporting verb.

Old Russian units (pood, verst, arshin, sazhen) are kept as transliterated words with a metric equivalent in parentheses at first use per chapter; товарищ / т. is always Comrade / 同志 / 同志, never a given name.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the young con man and co-protagonist; the narrator calls him by first name only here
terms.why_hard: Name spelling must be fixed once (Ostap, not Ostup/Astap); zh and ja transliterations must match every other page

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, the former marshal of the nobility, addressed throughout by name-and-patronymic
terms.why_hard: The patronymic is the formal, slightly mocking register; dropping it to 'Ippolit' or replacing with 'Mr Vorobyaninov' loses the joke of Ostap's exaggerated politeness

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: 'Glick Bros.', a (private, NEP-era) firm whose bedbug poison the hermit tries; 'бр.' is the pre-revolutionary trade abbreviation for 'братья'
terms.why_hard: A careless reader misses that 'бр.' means 'brothers'; the old-fashioned firm-name style signals a private NEP shop, which the rendering should keep

terms.gloss: Brand name of the pink bedbug poison, coined from 'клоп' (bedbug) plus a pharmaceutical suffix
terms.why_hard: Transliterating 'Klopin' loses the pun; the target reader needs to hear 'bedbug' in the brand name

terms.gloss: The hermit of Ostap's parable, called both 'отшельник' (hermit) and 'старец' (Orthodox 'elder', a venerated spiritual recluse)
terms.why_hard: 'старец' is not just 'old man'; it is a religious title with a Dostoevskian aura that Ostap uses mock-solemnly, so the two words must be rendered distinctly and consistently

terms.gloss: A dugout hut, half below ground, the traditional dwelling of a Russian forest hermit
terms.why_hard: 'Cabin' or 'hut' loses the underground image; 'dugout' alone in English suggests a sports bench or trench

terms.gloss: Porcini (boletus edulis) mushrooms, 'fat-bellied', the prized Russian forest mushroom; their appearance is the sign that life is beautiful
terms.why_hard: 'White mushrooms' is a literal false friend; the reader needs the prized, edible, plump connotation

proposed.ja: 太っちょのヤマドリタケ

terms.term: кучером конной базы Московского коммунального хозяйства
terms.gloss: Coachman at the horse depot of the Moscow Municipal Services (МКХ, the city utilities administration); the anticlimactic present-day job of the ex-hermit
terms.why_hard: The comic point is the drab bureaucratic full title; it must sound like an official Soviet job description, not be simplified to 'a cab driver in Moscow'

proposed.en: coachman at the horse depot of the Moscow Municipal Services
proposed.zh: 莫斯科市政公用事业局马匹站的车夫
proposed.ja: モスクワ市公共事業局馬車基地の御者

terms.gloss: Ostap's raspberry-coloured shoes, a recurring attribute of his dandyish poverty, which he calls 'my little friends'
terms.why_hard: The colour word must be fixed once (raspberry, not crimson/red/maroon) because the shoes reappear across the book

terms.gloss: He hummed a ceremonial fanfare ('туш', a short brass flourish played at award ceremonies) with his lips
terms.why_hard: 'Tush' or 'played a tune' misses that it is the official flourish for a solemn occasion, mocking his own story

proposed.en: hummed a ceremonial fanfare through his lips
proposed.zh: 用嘴唇吹了一段庆典号曲
proposed.ja: 唇で祝典ファンファーレを奏でた

terms.gloss: Chapter title and Ostap's mock-lyrical description of the widow Gritsatsuyeva; became a Russian proverb for a plump, ardent provincial woman
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered identically in the chapter heading and in Ostap's speech; 'hot woman' is too crude, 'sultry' keeps the parody of magazine prose

proposed.en: A sultry woman, a poet's dream
proposed.zh: 火辣的女人——诗人的梦想

terms.gloss: Madame Gritsatsuyeva, the widow Ostap courts for the chair; 'the diamond widow' because her chair may hold the jewels
terms.why_hard: The diminutive 'вдовушка' is affectionate-contemptuous; 'diamond widow' must be kept as the epithet that recurs in later chapters

proposed.en: the widow / the little diamond widow
proposed.ja: 未亡人 / ダイヤの未亡人ちゃん

terms.gloss: 'To marry her, as an honest man must' — the pre-revolutionary code that a seducer is obliged to marry; Ostap's joke that he has already spent the night
terms.why_hard: Literal 'like an honest man' is flat; the phrase implies the euphemism about what happened at the widow's, which the reader must catch

proposed.en: Now I'm honour-bound to marry her
proposed.zh: 现在我作为一个正派人非娶她不可了
proposed.ja: こうなった以上、紳士として結婚せざるを得ない

terms.gloss: 'Provincial artlessness' — Ostap's condescending Moscow view of the small-town widow's naive ardour
terms.why_hard: 'Spontaneity' or 'directness' misses the patronising capital-versus-province tone

terms.term: В центре … на периферии, на местах
terms.gloss: Soviet bureaucratic jargon: 'the Centre' (Moscow) versus 'the periphery' and 'the localities' (provincial bodies)
terms.why_hard: Ostap parodies party-report language about 'the localities'; a neutral 'in the provinces' erases the jargon

proposed.en: in the Centre … out on the periphery, in the localities
proposed.zh: 在中央……在边远地区、在地方上
proposed.ja: 中央では……周辺部の、地方では

terms.gloss: May Day, the Soviet public holiday when offices, including the registry office for marriages, are shut
terms.why_hard: Reader must understand this is a state holiday that closes the ZAGS (marriage registry), not a religious feast

proposed.zh: 五一劳动节——什么都关门
proposed.ja: メーデーで何もかも休みだ

terms.gloss: 'The session continues' — Ostap's recurring catchphrase, probably echoing the French Chamber president's 'La séance continue' after the 1893 Vaillant bomb; means 'business as usual, the plan goes on'
terms.why_hard: Must be fixed once for the whole book since it recurs; a naive 'the meeting goes on' loses its status as a slogan

terms.gloss: 'A summons from the Centre' — bureaucratic formula for being called to Moscow by higher authority, which Ostap invents as his exit story
terms.why_hard: 'Centre' capitalised is the Soviet term for central government; rendering it as 'from headquarters' or 'from the city' loses the pomposity

proposed.en: an urgent summons from the Centre
proposed.ja: 中央からの急な呼び出し

terms.gloss: The 'Little Sovnarkom', a standing commission of the Council of People's Commissars that prepared minor government business; a real body, name-dropped by Ostap for effect
terms.why_hard: Sovnarkom itself needs unpacking for the target reader; a transliteration alone is opaque, a full paraphrase kills the throwaway comedy

proposed.en: the Little Sovnarkom (the cabinet's junior commission)

terms.gloss: A roast chicken packed for the train journey — the standard Russian travel provision a devoted wife supplies
terms.why_hard: Reader should see the cosy domestic ritual Ostap is cynically scripting, not a live chick

proposed.en: a roast chicken for the road
proposed.ja: 旅の弁当の鶏の丸焼き

terms.gloss: Ostap's endearment to his raspberry shoes, stroked on the night table
terms.why_hard: Should be rendered with the same tender solemnity each time it recurs, matching the shoes' epithet

terms.gloss: The hermit's 'meaning of life' and 'worldly cares', the mock-religious vocabulary of the parable, in contrast with bedbug-hunting
terms.why_hard: The comic register depends on keeping the lofty churchly phrasing straight-faced so the bedbugs deflate it

proposed.en: the meaning of life / the cares of the world
proposed.zh: 生命的意义 / 尘世的烦忧
proposed.ja: 人生の意味 / 俗世の憂い

conventions: Dialogue: Russian dashes become double quotation marks in en, “” in zh and 「」 in ja; each Russian speech line maps to exactly one target line so the side-by-side alignment holds.

Names: transliterate once book-wide (Ostap, Ippolit Matveyevich, Vorobyaninov) with zh characters and ja katakana fixed in the glossary; keep name-and-patronymic in all three languages (ja without -san, since the patronymic already carries the formality).

Soviet institutions and acronyms (Sovnarkom, MKKh, 'the Centre') get a short in-line expansion on first appearance and the bare fixed rendering afterwards; the trailing wiki line 'Категория:Двенадцать стульев (Ильф и Петров)' is a source artefact and is not translated.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the young con man and co-protagonist; the narrator calls him Остап, Бендер or великий комбинатор interchangeably
terms.why_hard: The three designations must map to three stable renderings; zh/ja transliterations of Ostap vary between editions

terms.gloss: Ostap's surname, used by the narrator when the tone turns official or mock-military
terms.why_hard: Should not be normalised to 'Ostap' everywhere; the surname carries the mock-official register

terms.gloss: The narrator's recurring epithet for Ostap: the great schemer, master of 'combinations' (deals, swindles)
terms.why_hard: A literal 'combinator' means nothing in English; 'grand strategist' is the received rendering and must be used every time, since it is the book's signature phrase

terms.gloss: Alexander Yakovlevich, the завхоз of the old-women's home; the narrator alternates it with the diminutive Альхен
terms.why_hard: Name-plus-patronymic is a register marker (mock respect), not two separate people; ja/zh need a fixed transliteration of the patronymic

proposed.zh: 亚历山大·雅科夫列维奇
proposed.ja: アレクサンドル・ヤコヴレヴィチ

terms.gloss: Family diminutive of Alexander Yakovlevich, the shy embezzler ('the blue thief') who runs the home
terms.why_hard: Must be recognisably the same man as Александр Яковлевич; do not translate the diminutive into 'Sasha' or 'Alex'

terms.gloss: Chapter VIII title and Alkhen's epithet: a 'sky-blue' (i.e. gentle, blushing, sentimental) petty thief
terms.why_hard: Голубой here means innocent/pale-blue, not the modern slang sense 'gay'; воришка is a diminutive, so 'thief' alone loses the pathos

terms.gloss: Acronym for Stargorod Department of Social Security (Старгородский отдел социального обеспечения), which runs the old-women's home
terms.why_hard: The acronym is itself part of the satire of Soviet abbreviation; expanding it every time kills the joke, transliterating it explains nothing

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德社保局（斯塔尔社保）
proposed.ja: スタルゴロド社会保障局（スタルソベス）

terms.gloss: The Starsobes 2nd Home, a state old-age home for women housed in Vorobyaninov's former mansion
terms.why_hard: 'House No. 2' sounds like an address; the reader must understand it is an institution, and the same label must recur unchanged

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔社保局第二养老院
proposed.ja: スタルソベス第二養老院

terms.gloss: Adjective from собес (отдел социального обеспечения), the social-security office; here 'the собес locksmith'
terms.why_hard: Should be rendered consistently with Старсобес so the reader sees they are the same bureau

terms.gloss: Заведующий хозяйством: the supply-and-property manager of a Soviet institution, a NEP-era post proverbially open to petty theft
terms.why_hard: Not a janitor or caretaker; the word is an acronym-job with a whiff of embezzlement; recurs throughout the book

terms.gloss: Fire-safety inspector, the official Ostap impersonates while searching the house
terms.why_hard: The narrator keeps calling Ostap 'the inspector' with a straight face; the rendering must let the reader hold both identities

terms.gloss: Bureaucratic formula 'from the fire-safety standpoint', repeated as Ostap's running refrain on this page
terms.why_hard: The repetition is the joke; each recurrence must use the identical stilted phrase, not a fresh paraphrase

proposed.en: from the fire-safety point of view

terms.gloss: Toile du Nord, a cheap coarse grey cotton fabric; here used for slogans and the cook's cap
terms.why_hard: An obscure French loanword the Russian reader of 1928 knew as 'cheap institutional cloth'; transliterating it leaves the reader blank

terms.term: Духовой оркестр — путь к коллективному творчеству
terms.gloss: Wall slogan in the old-women's home, parodying agitprop slogans about collective culture
terms.why_hard: Must sound like a real slogan (stilted, hyphenated 'path to'), not like natural prose

proposed.en: THE BRASS BAND IS THE PATH TO COLLECTIVE CREATIVITY
proposed.zh: 铜管乐队是通向集体创造的道路
proposed.ja: 吹奏楽団は集団的創造への道

terms.gloss: Activities of a кружок, the Soviet amateur 'circle' (hobby/study group) every institution was expected to run
terms.why_hard: 'Circle' is opaque in English; 'club' is close but loses the mandatory-cultural-work flavour

terms.term: Александровского, ныне имени Пролетарских субботников, бульвара
terms.gloss: Stargorod boulevard renamed from Alexander Boulevard to 'Proletarian Subbotniks Boulevard'; a running joke about Soviet renaming
terms.why_hard: The 'formerly X, now Y' construction recurs across the book and must be rendered with one fixed pattern; субботник needs a gloss

proposed.en: Alexander Boulevard, now Proletarian Volunteer-Saturdays Boulevard
proposed.zh: 亚历山大林荫道（现称无产阶级星期六义务劳动林荫道）
proposed.ja: アレクサンドル大通り（現・プロレタリア土曜労働奉仕大通り）

terms.gloss: Unpaid 'voluntary' collective work on a Saturday, a Soviet civic ritual from 1919
terms.why_hard: A one-word transliteration means nothing to the target reader; needs a short in-line rendering fixed once for the whole book

terms.gloss: The mansion in Stargorod that belonged to Vorobyaninov before the revolution, now the old-women's home
terms.why_hard: Adjectival surname form; the surname must match the transliteration of Воробьянинов used everywhere else

proposed.zh: 沃罗比扬尼诺夫的府邸

terms.term: ореховый стул с гнутыми ножками, обитый светлым английским ситцем в цветочках
terms.gloss: The fixed description of the twelve Gambs chairs: walnut, curved legs, upholstered in light flowered English chintz
terms.why_hard: This description recurs verbatim through the book; wording must be frozen so the reader recognises the chair every time

proposed.en: a walnut chair with curved legs, upholstered in light flowered English chintz
proposed.zh: 一把弯腿胡桃木椅子，蒙着浅色英国印花布
proposed.ja: 曲がった脚の胡桃材の椅子、明るい花模様のイギリス更紗張り

terms.gloss: The word 'Feet' woven into institutional blankets to mark which end goes at the feet
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered as the single blunt woven word it is; the narrator calls it 'frightening', so no softening

terms.gloss: 'Running things on a military footing' — Alkhen's taste for barracks-style order (trunks pulled out exactly one third)
terms.why_hard: Dry mock-solemn phrasing; over-translating into 'military discipline' loses the bureaucratic ring

proposed.en: a military way of doing things

terms.gloss: Budget-speak: 'appropriations are allocated in insufficient quantity'; Alkhen's excuse for the grey cloth
terms.why_hard: Кредиты here means budget allocations, not loans; the joke is a shy man hiding behind office jargon

proposed.en: The allocations are released in insufficient quantity.
proposed.ja: 予算の交付が不十分な額でして。

terms.gloss: 'By God', a colloquial oath of sincerity, pre-revolutionary and slightly rustic
terms.why_hard: Recurs in many characters' speech; needs one fixed colloquial equivalent rather than ad hoc 'honestly'/'I swear'

terms.gloss: 'Fortress-like splendour' of the door springs and counterweights; the narrator's mock-heroic siege imagery (doors 'saluting', counterweights like cannonballs)
terms.why_hard: Крепостной here is 'fortress', not 'serf'; the military metaphor runs through the whole passage and should be kept coherent

conventions: Dialogue: Russian em-dash lines become double quotation marks in en, Chinese “ ” in zh, and 「 」 in ja; the dash itself is never carried over.

Soviet acronyms (Старсобес, собес, завхоз): give a short English/Chinese/Japanese meaning on first occurrence in the book, then use one fixed short rendering thereafter; never expand the acronym mid-sentence again.

Names: transliterate all personal names once for the whole book (Ostap Bender / Vorobyaninov / Alkhen), keep name-plus-patronymic where the Russian has it, and in Japanese use no honorific suffixes on narrator-voiced names.

meta.summary: object with keys [rank, terms, chapter_titles, conventions, page_types]

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the young con man and co-protagonist, here posing as a fire inspector
terms.why_hard: Spelling must stay fixed across the book (Ostap, not Ostip/Ostapp); zh/ja transliteration must match the one bound for the full name Остап Бендер

terms.gloss: Nickname of Alexander Yakovlevich, the thieving manager of the old women's home; the 'bashful thief' of the chapter title
terms.why_hard: It is the same man as Александр Яковлевич; the reader must see the link, and the soft, almost affectionate diminutive must not become a separate character

terms.gloss: Formal name-and-patronymic of Alkhen, used by the narrator with mock respect
terms.why_hard: Patronymic must be kept (the joke of the four Яковлевичи depends on it) and rendered identically wherever it recurs

proposed.zh: 亚历山大·雅科夫列维奇
proposed.ja: アレクサンドル・ヤコヴレヴィチ

terms.gloss: Alkhen's wife, who hand-lettered the dining-room slogans
terms.why_hard: Nearly identical to her husband's name; feminine endings must be preserved so the pair is distinguishable in all three languages

proposed.zh: 亚历山德拉·雅科夫列夫娜
proposed.ja: アレクサンドラ・ヤコヴレヴナ

terms.gloss: Alexandra Yakovlevna's 32-year-old 'second cousin once removed', a freeloader living in the home
terms.why_hard: Diminutive first name plus patronymic is itself a comic register (a grown man called 'Pasha'); keep it as is rather than expanding to Pavel

proposed.ja: パーシャ・エミーリエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Collective for Alkhen's four young brothers Isidor, Afanasy, Kirill and Oleg Yakovlevich
terms.why_hard: The narrator's plural of a patronymic is a running joke; each language needs one fixed collective form (not 'the Yakovlevich family')

terms.gloss: Soviet-style acronym: Stargorod department of social security (Старгородский отдел социального обеспечения)
terms.why_hard: Not a proper noun to transliterate blindly; the acronym is itself a parody of Soviet officialese and must be expanded once, then kept short and consistent

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德社保局（“斯塔尔索别斯”）
proposed.ja: スタルソベス（スタルゴロド社会保障局）

terms.gloss: Old women's home No. 2 run by the Stargorod social security department; the setting of chapters 7-8
terms.why_hard: Must not become 'house' or 'building'; it is an institution (an almshouse), and the number should be kept as part of its bureaucratic name

proposed.zh: 斯塔尔索别斯第二养老院
proposed.ja: スタルソベス第二養老院

terms.gloss: Generic short form: 'the welfare home', a state old people's home
terms.why_hard: Same institution as above in casual reference; the rendering must be visibly the short form of the full name, not a different place

terms.gloss: Заведующий хозяйством: the supply/housekeeping manager of a Soviet institution, Alkhen's actual post
terms.why_hard: A specific NEP-era job title; 'housekeeper' or 'janitor' loses the petty-official status that makes his theft possible

terms.gloss: Fire-safety inspector, the official role Ostap impersonates to search the home
terms.why_hard: Ostap's phrasing ('которую я в настоящий момент представляю') is deliberately pompous; the title must sound official in each language so his bluff reads as a bluff

terms.gloss: A conical tin foam fire extinguisher of the brand 'Eclair', the home's sole fire-safety item
terms.why_hard: Keep the brand name in quotation marks and translate the device type; the extinguisher recurs and 'sings' later, so its name must be stable

terms.gloss: Flea market, second-hand street market where junk is sold
terms.why_hard: Ostap's insult is that the extinguisher is junk bought second-hand; a neutral 'market' kills the jibe

terms.gloss: Bortniansky's hymn 'How Glorious Is Our Lord in Zion', the unofficial anthem of imperial Russia, once played by the Kremlin chimes
terms.why_hard: The joke is a Soviet fire extinguisher wheezing a Tsarist hymn; readers need a short in-line cue ('the old imperial hymn') or a brief note, not a literal title alone

proposed.en: 'How Glorious Is Our Lord in Zion' (the old imperial hymn)
proposed.zh: 《锡安的主何等荣耀》（旧帝俄圣歌）
proposed.ja: 「シオンにて我らの主は栄光あり」（旧帝政ロシアの聖歌）

terms.gloss: Toile du Nord: cheap grey cotton fabric used for institutional clothing; the home's inmates all wear it
terms.why_hard: Obsolete loanword; must be one fixed rendering because the narrator reuses it as an epithet for the home itself

terms.gloss: Mock-solemn 'palace of toile-du-Nord', i.e. the shabby old women's home
terms.why_hard: The high-style 'чертог' against the cheap fabric is the joke; both halves must survive and reuse the bound rendering of туальденор

terms.gloss: State-issue blankets stamped 'FEET' at one end so they are laid the right way round; a recurring image of Soviet institutional life
terms.why_hard: Literal 'legs' is wrong; the stamp should read as an absurd institutional label in caps, identically each time it recurs

terms.term: ТЩАТЕЛЬНО ПЕРЕЖЕВЫВАЯ ПИЩУ, ТЫ ПОМОГАЕШЬ ОБЩЕСТВУ
terms.gloss: Parody of 1920s Soviet hygiene posters; became a proverb and is quoted again later in the novel
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered as a poster slogan (caps, imperative-collective tone) and reused verbatim wherever it is quoted back

proposed.en: CHEW YOUR FOOD THOROUGHLY AND YOU HELP SOCIETY
proposed.zh: 细嚼慢咽，即是为社会做贡献
proposed.ja: 食物をよく噛むことは社会への貢献である

terms.gloss: Dining-room slogan 'Meat is harmful', justifying the absence of meat in the home
terms.why_hard: Terseness is the joke; a softened 'meat is unhealthy' loses the bureaucratic flatness

terms.gloss: Half a Russian pound (about 205 g) of meat, in the egg slogan
terms.why_hard: Do not convert to grams inside a poster slogan; keep 'half a pound' and note the Russian pound only if a unit convention is bound book-wide

terms.gloss: Tiny Black Sea sprat (kilka), the cheapest salted fish of the era
terms.why_hard: Pasha's feat is eating two kilos of the cheapest fish there is; 'sardines' or 'herring' make it sound like a treat

terms.gloss: Institutional term 'wards/inmates' applied ironically to the old women of the home
terms.why_hard: Literally 'pupils'; the narrator borrows orphanage vocabulary for old women, so the rendering must sound bureaucratic rather than warm

terms.gloss: Chapter VIII title: Alkhen, the 'bashful little thief' who blushes while stealing
terms.why_hard: голубой here means innocent/tender, not 'blue' and not the modern 'gay'; the diminutive -ишка is affectionate contempt

terms.gloss: Coarse 'stuff their faces / get their fill'; the old women's grumbling register
terms.why_hard: The old women speak low and blunt, the narrator high and dry; the register gap must be kept, not levelled

conventions: Dialogue: replace Russian em-dash dialogue with quotation marks (en “ ”, zh “ ”, ja 「 」); keep the narrator's interpolated asides ('заявил он', 'подтвердил Остап') in their original position.

Names: keep name + patronymic wherever the Russian has it; en uses simplified Library-of-Congress spelling without diacritics, zh the standard Xinhua transliteration table, ja katakana with the interpunct; ja adds no honorifics (no さん/氏).

Soviet acronyms and job titles (Старсобес, собес, завхоз): give a descriptive rendering on first appearance in the book, then a fixed short form; no footnotes for these, notes reserved for allusions like the hymn.
